author: pliny
title: The Eruption of Vesuvius: Pliny the Elder Sets Out
summary: Writing to Tacitus, Pliny agrees to describe his uncle's death so that it may be handed down to posterity, calling him fortunate both in the manner of his death and in having Tacitus to record it. His uncle was at Misenum in command of the fleet when, on 24 August at about the seventh hour, his mother pointed out a cloud of unusual size and appearance. It rose like a pine tree, on a very long trunk, spreading into branches, sometimes white and sometimes dirty and spotted. As a scholar he thought it important enough to inspect more closely and ordered a light vessel made ready. As he was leaving the house he received a note from Rectina, wife of Tascius, terrified by the danger, begging rescue since her villa lay at the foot of the mountain and escape was only possible by sea. He changed his plan and carried out with the greatest spirit what he had begun as a scholar: he launched the quadriremes and steered straight for the danger that others were fleeing, dictating and taking notes as he went. Ash was already falling, hotter and thicker as they approached, then pumice and blackened stones burnt by the fire; the sea shallowed suddenly and the shore was blocked by debris from the mountain. He hesitated briefly whether to turn back, then told the helmsman that fortune favours the brave and to make for Pomponianus.
context: The eruption of 24 August (or, on some manuscripts and modern arguments, 24 October) 79 CE destroyed Pompeii and Herculaneum. Pliny the Elder, author of the Naturalis Historia, was prefect of the fleet at Misenum. The letter is our only eyewitness-derived account of the eruption and gives its name to 'Plinian' eruptions. Note fortes fortuna iuvat — a proverb Pliny puts in his uncle's mouth at the decisive moment.

lines.latin: Petis ut tibi avunculi mei exitum scribam, quo verius tradere posteris possis. Gratias ago; nam video morti eius si celebretur a te immortalem gloriam esse propositam.
lines.english: You ask that I write to you [about] the death of my uncle, so that you can hand it down more truly to posterity. I give thanks; for I see that for his death, if it is celebrated by you, immortal glory has been set before [it].

lines.latin: Quamvis enim pulcherrimarum clade terrarum, ut populi ut urbes memorabili casu, quasi semper victurus occiderit, quamvis ipse plurima opera et mansura condiderit, multum tamen perpetuitati eius scriptorum tuorum aeternitas addet.
lines.english: For although he died in the destruction of the most beautiful lands, as peoples [did], as cities [did], by a memorable disaster, as though about to live forever, although he himself founded very many and lasting works, nevertheless the eternity of your writings will add much to his perpetuity.

lines.latin: Equidem beatos puto, quibus deorum munere datum est aut facere scribenda aut scribere legenda, beatissimos vero quibus utrumque. Horum in numero avunculus meus et suis libris et tuis erit. Quo libentius suscipio, deposco etiam quod iniungis.
lines.english: Indeed, I consider fortunate those to whom, by the gift of the gods, it has been given either to do things worth writing or to write things worth reading, but most fortunate those to whom both [have been given]. In the number of these my uncle will be, both through his own books and through yours. For which reason I undertake the more willingly, I even demand, what you enjoin.

lines.latin: Erat Miseni classemque imperio praesens regebat. Nonum Kal. Septembres hora fere septima mater mea indicat ei apparere nubem inusitata et magnitudine et specie.
lines.english: He was at Misenum and was commanding the fleet in person with full authority. On the ninth day before the Kalends of September, at about the seventh hour, my mother points out to him that a cloud is appearing, unusual both in size and in appearance.

lines.latin: Usus ille sole, mox frigida, gustaverat iacens studebatque; poscit soleas, ascendit locum ex quo maxime miraculum illud conspici poterat. Nubes — incertum procul intuentibus ex quo monte; Vesuvium fuisse postea cognitum est — oriebatur, cuius similitudinem et formam non alia magis arbor quam pinus expresserit.
lines.english: He, having enjoyed the sun, then cold [water], had eaten lying down and was studying; he asks for his sandals, he climbs to a place from which that marvel could best be seen. A cloud — it was uncertain to those looking from afar from which mountain; it was learned afterward to have been Vesuvius — was rising, whose likeness and shape no other tree would have expressed more than a pine.

lines.latin: Nam longissimo velut trunco elata in altum quibusdam ramis diffundebatur, credo quia recenti spiritu evecta, dein senescente eo destituta aut etiam pondere suo victa in latitudinem vanescebat, candida interdum, interdum sordida et maculosa prout terram cineremve sustulerat.
lines.english: For, carried up on high as if on a very long trunk, it was spreading out into some branches, I believe because, carried up by a fresh blast, then abandoned as that [blast] grew old, or even overcome by its own weight, it was vanishing into breadth, sometimes white, sometimes dirty and spotted, according as it had carried up earth or ash.

lines.latin: Magnum propiusque noscendum ut eruditissimo viro visum. Iubet liburnicam aptari; mihi si venire una vellem facit copiam; respondi studere me malle, et forte ipse quod scriberem dederat.
lines.english: It seemed [something] great and to be learned about more closely, as [it would] to a most learned man. He orders a Liburnian galley to be made ready; he gives me the opportunity, if I wanted to come along; I answered that I preferred to study, and by chance he himself had given [me something] which I was to write.

lines.latin: Egrediebatur domo; accipit codicillos Rectinae Tasci imminenti periculo exterritae — nam villa eius subiacebat, nec ulla nisi navibus fuga -: ut se tanto discrimini eriperet orabat.
lines.english: He was leaving the house; he receives a note from Rectina, [wife] of Tascus, terrified by the threatening danger — for her villa lay below, and [there was] no escape except by ships —: she was begging that he snatch her from so great a danger.

lines.latin: Vertit ille consilium et quod studioso animo incohaverat obit maximo. Deducit quadriremes, ascendit ipse non Rectinae modo sed multis — erat enim frequens amoenitas orae — laturus auxilium.
lines.english: He changes his plan, and what he had begun with a studious mind he carries out with the greatest [mind]. He launches quadriremes; he himself goes on board, about to bring help not only to Rectina but to many — for the charming shore was crowded [with people].

lines.latin: Properat illuc unde alii fugiunt, rectumque cursum recta gubernacula in periculum tenet adeo solutus metu, ut omnes illius mali motus omnes figuras ut deprenderat oculis dictaret enotaretque.
lines.english: He hurries to that place from which others flee, and he holds a straight course, a straight rudder, into the danger, so free from fear that he dictated and noted down all the movements of that evil, all its shapes, as he had caught them with his eyes.

lines.latin: Iam navibus cinis incidebat, quo propius accederent, calidior et densior; iam pumices etiam nigrique et ambusti et fracti igne lapides; iam vadum subitum ruinaque montis litora obstantia. Cunctatus paulum an retro flecteret, mox gubernatori ut ita faceret monenti 'Fortes' inquit 'fortuna iuvat: Pomponianum pete.'
lines.english: Already ash was falling on the ships, hotter and denser the closer they approached; already even pumice stones and black stones, scorched and broken by fire; already a sudden shoal, and shores blocking [the way] with the debris of the mountain. Having hesitated a little whether he should turn back, soon to the helmsman warning that he do so he said, “Fortune helps the brave: head for Pomponianus.”

lines.latin: Stabiis erat diremptus sinu medio — nam sensim circumactis curvatisque litoribus mare infunditur -; ibi quamquam nondum periculo appropinquante, conspicuo tamen et cum cresceret proximo, sarcinas contulerat in naves, certus fugae si contrarius ventus resedisset. Quo tunc avunculus meus secundissimo invectus, complectitur trepidantem consolatur hortatur, utque timorem eius sua securitate leniret, deferri in balineum iubet; lotus accubat cenat, aut hilaris aut — quod aeque magnum — similis hilari.
lines.english: He was at Stabiae, separated by the middle of the bay — for the sea pours in on shores gradually curved and bent around —; there, although the danger was not yet approaching, yet [it was] visible and, when it should grow, very near, he had gathered his baggage onto ships, set on flight if the contrary wind died down. Carried in then by this [wind], most favorable, my uncle embraces him, trembling, consoles him, encourages him, and so that he might soothe his fear by his own calm, he orders [himself] to be carried down into the bath; having bathed, he reclines, he dines, either cheerful or — what is equally great — like one cheerful.

author: pliny
title: The Eruption of Vesuvius: The Younger Pliny at Misenum
summary: Pliny takes up Tacitus' request for an account of what he himself endured at Misenum after his uncle's departure. For several days there had been earth tremors, less alarming because they are common in Campania; but that night they grew so violent that everything seemed not so much shaken as overturned. His mother came to his room as he was rising to wake her; they sat in the forecourt. Pliny, then seventeen, called for a volume of Livy and went on reading and even making extracts as if at leisure. A friend of his uncle's, recently arrived from Spain, rebuked them both — the mother for her patience, Pliny for his unconcern — but he went on reading. By the first hour of day the light was still faint and doubtful; the buildings around were shaking, and though they were in the open the space was narrow and collapse was certain. Only then did they decide to leave the town, followed by a stricken crowd that pressed on them and drove them forward. Once clear of the buildings they stopped, and there experienced many strange and fearful things: the carts they had ordered out ran in opposite directions on perfectly level ground and would not stay still even when wedged with stones; the sea appeared to be sucked back and driven away by the earthquake, the shore had widened, and many sea creatures were stranded on dry sand.
context: Written as a companion to 6.16, at Tacitus' request, and giving the civilian experience of the eruption. The detail of the seventeen-year-old Pliny calmly excerpting Livy in the middle of an earthquake is the letter's most famous touch — self-presentation as much as reportage. The description of the sea withdrawing is a recognisable account of tsunami behaviour.

lines.latin: Ais te adductum litteris quas exigenti tibi de morte avunculi mei scripsi, cupere cognoscere, quos ego Miseni relictus — id enim ingressus abruperam — non solum metus verum etiam casus pertulerim. 'Quamquam animus meminisse horret, ... incipiam.'
lines.english: You say that, led by the letter which I wrote to you, as you demanded, about the death of my uncle, you desire to learn what not only fears but also misfortunes I, left at Misenum (for having begun that I had broken off), endured. “Although my mind shudders to remember, … I will begin.”

lines.latin: Profecto avunculo ipse reliquum tempus studiis — ideo enim remanseram — impendi; mox balineum cena somnus inquietus et brevis.
lines.english: My uncle having set out, I myself spent the remaining time on studies — for that was why I had stayed behind —; soon a bath, dinner, sleep restless and brief.

lines.latin: Praecesserat per multos dies tremor terrae, minus formidolosus quia Campaniae solitus; illa vero nocte ita invaluit, ut non moveri omnia sed verti crederentur.
lines.english: There had preceded for many days a trembling of the earth, less frightening because [it is] usual for Campania; but on that night it grew so strong that all things were believed not to be moved but to be overturned.

lines.latin: Irrupit cubiculum meum mater; surgebam invicem, si quiesceret excitaturus. Resedimus in area domus, quae mare a tectis modico spatio dividebat.
lines.english: My mother burst into my bedroom; I was getting up in turn, about to wake [her] if she was sleeping. We sat down in the courtyard of the house, which separated the sea from the buildings by a modest space.

lines.latin: Dubito, constantiam vocare an imprudentiam debeam — agebam enim duodevicensimum annum -: posco librum Titi Livi, et quasi per otium lego atque etiam ut coeperam excerpo. Ecce amicus avunculi qui nuper ad eum ex Hispania venerat, ut me et matrem sedentes, me vero etiam legentem videt, illius patientiam securitatem meam corripit. Nihilo segnius ego intentus in librum.
lines.english: I hesitate whether I ought to call it steadiness or imprudence — for I was spending my eighteenth year —: I ask for a book of Titus Livy, and as if at leisure I read and even, as I had begun, make excerpts. Look, a friend of my uncle who had recently come to him from Spain, when he sees me and my mother sitting, and me even reading, rebukes her patience [and] my carelessness. No less diligently [was] I intent on the book.

lines.latin: Iam hora diei prima, et adhuc dubius et quasi languidus dies. Iam quassatis circumiacentibus tectis, quamquam in aperto loco, angusto tamen, magnus et certus ruinae metus.
lines.english: Now [it was] the first hour of the day, and the daylight [was] still doubtful and as if faint. Now, the surrounding buildings having been shaken, although [we were] in an open place, yet a narrow one, [there was] a great and certain fear of collapse.

lines.latin: Tum demum excedere oppido visum; sequitur vulgus attonitum, quodque in pavore simile prudentiae, alienum consilium suo praefert, ingentique agmine abeuntes premit et impellit.
lines.english: Then at last it seemed best to leave the town; a stunned crowd follows, and, what in panic is like prudence, prefers another’s plan to its own, and with a huge column presses and pushes [us] as we go away.

lines.latin: Egressi tecta consistimus. Multa ibi miranda, multas formidines patimur. Nam vehicula quae produci iusseramus, quamquam in planissimo campo, in contrarias partes agebantur, ac ne lapidibus quidem fulta in eodem vestigio quiescebant.
lines.english: Having gone out beyond the buildings, we stop. There we endure many things to be wondered at, many terrors. For the carriages which we had ordered to be brought out, although on the flattest ground, were being driven in opposite directions, and not even propped with stones were they staying still in the same track.

lines.latin: Praeterea mare in se resorberi et tremore terrae quasi repelli videbamus. Certe processerat litus, multaque animalia maris siccis harenis detinebat. Ab altero latere nubes atra et horrenda, ignei spiritus tortis vibratisque discursibus rupta, in longas flammarum figuras dehiscebat; fulguribus illae et similes et maiores erant.
lines.english: Besides, we were seeing the sea sucked back into itself and as if driven back by the trembling of the earth. Certainly the shore had advanced, and was holding many sea creatures on the dry sands. On the other side a black and dreadful cloud, broken by twisted and quivering rushes of fiery breath, was gaping open into long shapes of flames; these were both like lightning flashes and greater.

lines.latin: Tum vero idem ille ex Hispania amicus acrius et instantius 'Si frater' inquit 'tuus, tuus avunculus vivit, vult esse vos salvos; si periit, superstites voluit. Proinde quid cessatis evadere?' Respondimus non commissuros nos ut de salute illius incerti nostrae consuleremus.
lines.english: Then indeed that same friend from Spain [said] more sharply and more urgently, “If your brother, your uncle, is alive, he wants you to be safe; if he has died, he wanted you to survive. So why do you hesitate to escape?” We answered that we would not allow ourselves, uncertain about his safety, to look after our own.

author: pliny
title: The Eruption of Vesuvius: Flight from Misenum
summary: On the other side a black and dreadful cloud, broken by twisting flashes of fire, gapes open in long shapes of flame like lightning but larger. The Spanish friend urges them more sharply to flee, saying that if his brother and uncle survives he wants them safe, and departs at speed. Soon the cloud descends to the earth and covers the sea, hiding Capri and Misenum. Pliny's mother begs, urges and orders him to escape somehow, saying a young man can, while she, weighed down by age and body, will die content if she has not been the cause of his death; he replies that he will not be saved without her, takes her hand and forces her to quicken her pace. Ash begins to fall, then darkness — not like a moonless or cloudy night but like a closed room with the lamp put out. They hear women wailing, children crying, men shouting; some call for their parents, others for their children or wives, recognising them by voice; some pray for death out of fear of death; many raise their hands to the gods, but more conclude that there are no gods anywhere and that this is the world's last, eternal night. At last the darkness thins into smoke or cloud, real day returns, the sun even shines but sallow as in an eclipse, and everything appears changed and buried deep in ash as in snow. They return to Misenum and pass an anxious night between hope and fear, fear prevailing, since the earth still trembles. Pliny closes by insisting that these are not matters for history and that Tacitus need not put them in his work.
context: The closing lines — non historia digna, and the reminder that Tacitus asked — are a conventional modesty topos, and worth noticing as an epistolary convention rather than a statement of fact. The scene of Pliny refusing to abandon his mother is a deliberate echo of Aeneas carrying Anchises from Troy, which makes it a natural comparison passage with the Aeneid.

lines.latin: Non moratus ultra proripit se effusoque cursu periculo aufertur. Nec multo post illa nubes descendere in terras, operire maria; cinxerat Capreas et absconderat, Miseni quod procurrit abstulerat.
lines.english: Not having delayed further, he rushes out and in headlong flight is carried away from the danger. Not much later that cloud [began] to descend onto the lands, to cover the seas; it had surrounded and hidden Capri, it had taken away [from sight] the promontory of Misenum which juts out.

lines.latin: Tum mater orare hortari iubere, quoquo modo fugerem; posse enim iuvenem, se et annis et corpore gravem bene morituram, si mihi causa mortis non fuisset. Ego contra salvum me nisi una non futurum; dein manum eius amplexus addere gradum cogo. Paret aegre incusatque se, quod me moretur.
lines.english: Then my mother [began] to beg, to urge, to order that I flee in whatever way; for [she said] that a young man could, that she, heavy both in years and in body, would die well, if she had not been the cause of death for me. I, on the contrary, [said] that I would not be safe unless together [with her]; then, having grasped her hand, I force her to add pace. She obeys reluctantly and accuses herself because she is delaying me.

lines.latin: Iam cinis, adhuc tamen rarus. Respicio: densa caligo tergis imminebat, quae nos torrentis modo infusa terrae sequebatur. 'Deflectamus' inquam 'dum videmus, ne in via strati comitantium turba in tenebris obteramur.'
lines.english: Now ash, yet still sparse. I look back: a thick darkness was threatening at our backs, which, poured over the earth in the manner of a torrent, was following us. “Let us turn aside,” I say, “while we can see, so that we are not, knocked down in the road, trampled in the darkness by the crowd of those accompanying [us].”

lines.latin: Vix consideramus, et nox — non qualis illunis aut nubila, sed qualis in locis clausis lumine exstincto. Audires ululatus feminarum, infantum quiritatus, clamores virorum; alii parentes alii liberos alii coniuges vocibus requirebant, vocibus noscitabant; hi suum casum, illi suorum miserabantur; erant qui metu mortis mortem precarentur;
lines.english: Scarcely had we sat down, and [there was] night — not such as [when it is] moonless or cloudy, but such as in closed places with the light put out. You could hear the shrieks of women, the wailing of infants, the shouts of men; some were seeking parents, others children, others spouses with their voices, [and] were recognizing [them] by their voices; these were pitying their own misfortune, those that of their loved ones; there were those who, from fear of death, prayed for death;

lines.latin: multi ad deos manus tollere, plures nusquam iam deos ullos aeternamque illam et novissimam noctem mundo interpretabantur. Nec defuerunt qui fictis mentitisque terroribus vera pericula augerent. Aderant qui Miseni illud ruisse illud ardere falso sed credentibus nuntiabant.
lines.english: many [began] to raise their hands to the gods; more were interpreting that there were no longer any gods anywhere and that [this was] that eternal and final night for the world. Nor were there lacking those who increased real dangers with invented and lying terrors. There were present those who were announcing that at Misenum this had collapsed, that was burning — falsely, but to people believing [them].

lines.latin: Paulum reluxit, quod non dies nobis, sed adventantis ignis indicium videbatur. Et ignis quidem longius substitit; tenebrae rursus cinis rursus, multus et gravis. Hunc identidem assurgentes excutiebamus; operti alioqui atque etiam oblisi pondere essemus.
lines.english: It grew light a little, which seemed to us not daylight but a sign of approaching fire. And the fire indeed stopped rather far off; darkness again, ash again, much and heavy. Rising up again and again we were shaking this off; otherwise we would have been covered and even crushed by the weight.

lines.latin: Possem gloriari non gemitum mihi, non vocem parum fortem in tantis periculis excidisse, nisi me cum omnibus, omnia mecum perire misero, magno tamen mortalitatis solacio credidissem.
lines.english: I could boast that not a groan, not a word too little brave fell from me in such great dangers, if I had not believed that I was perishing with all things, and all things with me, a wretched but nevertheless great consolation for mortality.

lines.latin: Tandem illa caligo tenuata quasi in fumum nebulamve discessit; mox dies verus; sol etiam effulsit, luridus tamen qualis esse cum deficit solet. Occursabant trepidantibus adhuc oculis mutata omnia altoque cinere tamquam nive obducta.
lines.english: At last that darkness, thinned, departed as if into smoke or mist; soon [came] real daylight; the sun even shone out, pale however, such as it usually is when it is eclipsed. All things met our still trembling eyes changed, and covered with deep ash as if with snow.

lines.latin: Regressi Misenum curatis utcumque corporibus suspensam dubiamque noctem spe ac metu exegimus. Metus praevalebat; nam et tremor terrae perseverabat, et plerique lymphati terrificis vaticinationibus et sua et aliena mala ludificabantur.
lines.english: Having returned to Misenum, our bodies having been cared for somehow, we spent an anxious and doubtful night in hope and fear. Fear prevailed; for both the trembling of the earth was continuing, and very many, frenzied, were mocking both their own and others’ misfortunes with terrifying prophecies.

lines.latin: Nobis tamen ne tunc quidem, quamquam et expertis periculum et exspectantibus, abeundi consilium, donec de avunculo nuntius. Haec nequaquam historia digna non scripturus leges et tibi scilicet qui requisisti imputabis, si digna ne epistula quidem videbuntur. Vale.
lines.english: To us, however, not even then, although we had both experienced danger and were expecting it, [was there] a plan of leaving, until [there came] news about my uncle. These things, by no means worthy of history, you will read without intending to write [them], and you will surely blame yourself, who asked for them, if they seem not even worthy of a letter. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: The Eruption of Vesuvius: The Death of Pliny the Elder
summary: At Pomponianus' house at Stabiae Pliny the Elder embraces his frightened friend, comforts him, and — to allay his fear by his own unconcern — asks to be taken to the bath, dines cheerfully or with a convincing show of cheerfulness, and then sleeps a genuine sleep, his breathing audible to those outside the door. Meanwhile broad sheets of flame and tall fires blaze from Vesuvius, their glare heightened by the darkness of the night; Pliny insists they are only fires left burning in abandoned farmhouses. When the courtyard begins to fill with ash and stones, so that a longer delay would have trapped him, he is woken and joins the others in debate. They decide to tie pillows over their heads with cloths as protection against falling stones and go down to the shore. Day had come elsewhere but there it was still night, blacker and thicker than any night, relieved only by torches; the sea was still too wild to embark. Pliny lies down on a spread sheet, calls repeatedly for cold water and drinks it. Then flames and a smell of sulphur put the others to flight and rouse him. Leaning on two slaves he stands up and immediately falls, his breathing blocked, Pliny supposes, by the thick fumes, since he had a naturally weak windpipe. When daylight returned on the third day his body was found intact, unharmed and clothed as he had been, looking more like a sleeper than a dead man.
context: The composure of the elder Pliny — bathing, dining, sleeping while the mountain burns — is carefully constructed to present a Roman death of the highest kind. Pliny is writing for publication, to Tacitus the historian, and the letter should be read as a consciously literary artefact as well as a source.

lines.latin: Interim e Vesuvio monte pluribus locis latissimae flammae altaque incendia relucebant, quorum fulgor et claritas tenebris noctis excitabatur. Ille agrestium trepidatione ignes relictos desertasque villas per solitudinem ardere in remedium formidinis dictitabat. Tum se quieti dedit et quievit verissimo quidem somno; nam meatus animae, qui illi propter amplitudinem corporis gravior et sonantior erat, ab iis qui limini obversabantur audiebatur.
lines.english: Meanwhile from Mount Vesuvius, in very many places, very broad flames and high fires were shining, whose brilliance and brightness was heightened by the darkness of the night. He kept saying, as a remedy for fear, that fires left behind in the panic of the country people and abandoned villas were burning in the solitude. Then he gave himself to rest and rested in a very true sleep indeed; for his breathing, which for him because of the size of his body was rather heavy and loud, was heard by those who were moving about at the threshold.

lines.latin: Sed area ex qua diaeta adibatur ita iam cinere mixtisque pumicibus oppleta surrexerat, ut si longior in cubiculo mora, exitus negaretur. Excitatus procedit, seque Pomponiano ceterisque qui pervigilaverant reddit.
lines.english: But the courtyard from which the suite was approached had risen, so filled already with ash and mixed pumice stones, that if [there were] a longer delay in the bedroom, exit would be denied. Having been awakened, he comes out and returns himself to Pomponianus and the others who had stayed awake all night.

lines.latin: In commune consultant, intra tecta subsistant an in aperto vagentur. Nam crebris vastisque tremoribus tecta nutabant, et quasi emota sedibus suis nunc huc nunc illuc abire aut referri videbantur.
lines.english: They consult in common whether they should stay within the buildings or wander in the open. For the buildings were tottering with frequent and huge tremors and, as if dislodged from their foundations, they seemed to go away, now this way, now that, or to be brought back.

lines.latin: Sub dio rursus quamquam levium exesorumque pumicum casus metuebatur, quod tamen periculorum collatio elegit; et apud illum quidem ratio rationem, apud alios timorem timor vicit. Cervicalia capitibus imposita linteis constringunt; id munimentum adversus incidentia fuit.
lines.english: Under the open sky, on the other hand, the fall of pumice stones, although light and porous, was feared, which, however, a comparison of dangers chose; and with him indeed reason overcame reason, with the others fear [overcame] fear. They tie pillows placed on their heads with linen cloths; that was a protection against things falling.

lines.latin: Iam dies alibi, illic nox omnibus noctibus nigrior densiorque; quam tamen faces multae variaque lumina solvebant. Placuit egredi in litus, et ex proximo adspicere, ecquid iam mare admitteret; quod adhuc vastum et adversum permanebat.
lines.english: Now [it was] day elsewhere; there [it was] night, blacker and denser than all nights, which, however, many torches and various lights were relieving. It was decided to go out onto the shore, and to look from close by whether the sea would now allow anything; which was still remaining vast and hostile.

lines.latin: Ibi super abiectum linteum recubans semel atque iterum frigidam aquam poposcit hausitque. Deinde flammae flammarumque praenuntius odor sulpuris alios in fugam vertunt, excitant illum.
lines.english: There, lying down on a linen cloth thrown down, once and again he asked for cold water and drank it. Then flames, and the smell of sulfur, forewarning of flames, turn the others to flight [and] rouse him.

lines.latin: Innitens servolis duobus assurrexit et statim concidit, ut ego colligo, crassiore caligine spiritu obstructo, clausoque stomacho qui illi natura invalidus et angustus et frequenter aestuans erat.
lines.english: Leaning on two little slaves he rose up and immediately collapsed, as I gather, his breathing having been blocked by the rather thick darkness and his windpipe closed, which for him was by nature weak and narrow and often inflamed.

lines.latin: Ubi dies redditus — is ab eo quem novissime viderat tertius -, corpus inventum integrum illaesum opertumque ut fuerat indutus: habitus corporis quiescenti quam defuncto similior.
lines.english: When daylight was returned — that was the third from the one which he had seen last —, his body was found intact, unharmed, and covered as he had been dressed: the appearance of the body [was] more like one resting than one dead.

lines.latin: Interim Miseni ego et mater — sed nihil ad historiam, nec tu aliud quam de exitu eius scire voluisti. Finem ergo faciam.
lines.english: Meanwhile at Misenum I and my mother — but [this is] nothing to history, nor did you want to know anything other than about his death. I will therefore make an end.

lines.latin: Unum adiciam, omnia me quibus interfueram quaeque statim, cum maxime vera memorantur, audieram, persecutum. Tu potissima excerpes; aliud est enim epistulam aliud historiam, aliud amico aliud omnibus scribere. Vale.
lines.english: I will add one thing, that I have followed through all the things at which I had been present and which I had heard immediately, when things are recalled most truly. You will excerpt the most important things; for it is one thing to write a letter, another a history, one thing [to write] to a friend, another to everyone. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: To Calpurnia: Anxiety in Her Absence
summary: Pliny writes that he has never complained more about his own affairs, which prevent him from following Calpurnia as she sets out for Campania for her health, or from following immediately. He particularly wants to be with her now to see with his own eyes how much strength and how much flesh she is gaining, and whether she is bearing the ease of her retreat and the abundance of the region without harm. Even if she were well he would be anxious in her absence, since it brings suspense and fear to hear nothing for a time about one you love deeply. As it is, worry about her health torments him with vague and various fears: he fears everything, imagines everything, and, as anxious people do, imagines above all the things he most dreads. He therefore asks her all the more urgently to write to him once or even twice a day, since he will be less anxious while he is reading, and will begin to fear again as soon as he has read.
context: One of three surviving letters from Pliny to his young third wife Calpurnia, and among the very few expressions of conjugal affection in classical Latin prose. The letters are nonetheless published literary compositions, and the rhetoric of anxiety is carefully built — note the balanced omnia timeo, omnia imaginor.

lines.latin: Numquam sum magis de occupationibus meis questus, quae me non sunt passae aut proficiscentem te valetudinis causa in Campaniam prosequi aut profectam e vestigio subsequi.
lines.english: Never have I complained more about my business affairs, which have not allowed me either to accompany you as you set out into Campania for the sake of your health or to follow you immediately after you had set out.

lines.latin: Nunc enim praecipue simul esse cupiebam, ut oculis meis crederem quid viribus quid corpusculo apparares, ecquid denique secessus voluptates regionisque abundantiam inoffensa transmitteres.
lines.english: For now especially I was desiring to be together, so that I might believe my own eyes [about] what you were gaining for your strength, what for your little body, whether, finally, you were passing through the pleasures of your retreat and the abundance of the region unharmed.

lines.latin: Equidem etiam fortem te non sine cura desiderarem; est enim suspensum et anxium de eo quem ardentissime diligas interdum nihil scire.
lines.english: Indeed, even [if you were] strong, I would miss you not without anxiety; for it is suspenseful and anxious to know nothing at times about one whom you love most ardently.

lines.latin: Nunc vero me cum absentiae tum infirmitatis tuae ratio incerta et varia sollicitudine exterret. Vereor omnia, imaginor omnia, quaeque natura metuentium est, ea maxime mihi quae maxime abominor fingo.
lines.english: But now the consideration both of your absence and of your illness terrifies me with uncertain and varied worry. I fear all things, I imagine all things, and, which is the nature of those who are afraid, I invent for myself those things most which I most dread.

lines.latin: Quo impensius rogo, ut timori meo cottidie singulis vel etiam binis epistulis consulas. Ero enim securior dum lego, statimque timebo cum legero. Vale.
lines.english: All the more earnestly I ask that you look after my fear daily with one or even two letters. For I will be calmer while I read, and immediately I will be afraid when I have read. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: To Calpurnia: Reading Her Letters
summary: Calpurnia writes that she is much affected by Pliny's absence, and that her one comfort is to hold his books in his place and often to put them in the place he would occupy. Pliny replies that he is glad she misses him and glad she rests in that solace, and that he for his part reads her letters again and again and takes them up repeatedly as if they were new — but is set on fire the more sharply by longing. He asks her to write as often as she can, though her letters delight him in a way that also tortures him.
context: A very short letter, and a striking piece of self-conscious epistolary theory: the letter stands in for the absent person, and reading it both consoles and inflames. Calpurnia's placing of his writings beside her is one of the few glimpses in Latin of a woman's reading practice, though it reaches us only through Pliny's framing.

lines.latin: Scribis te absentia mea non mediocriter affici unumque habere solacium, quod pro me libellos meos teneas, saepe etiam in vestigio meo colloces.
lines.english: You write that you are affected not moderately by my absence and that you have one comfort, that in place of me you hold my little books [and] often even set them in my place.

lines.latin: Gratum est quod nos requiris, gratum quod his fomentis acquiescis; invicem ego epistulas tuas lectito atque identidem in manus quasi novas sumo.
lines.english: It is pleasing that you miss us, pleasing that you find rest in these remedies; in turn I read and reread your letters and again and again take them into my hands as if new.

lines.latin: Sed eo magis ad desiderium tui accendor: nam cuius litterae tantum habent suavitatis, huius sermonibus quantum dulcedinis inest! Tu tamen quam frequentissime scribe, licet hoc ita me delectet ut torqueat. Vale.
lines.english: But by this I am inflamed more to longing for you: for of [the one] whose letters have so much sweetness, how much delight is in her conversations! You, however, write as often as possible, although this delights me in such a way that it torments [me]. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: Ghosts: Curtius Rufus and the Haunted House
summary: Pliny writes to Sura, taking advantage of their shared leisure to ask whether he thinks ghosts exist, having their own shape and some divine power, or whether they are empty and unreal and take form only from our fear. He is inclined to believe they exist, chiefly because of what he has heard about Curtius Rufus. While still of low station and unknown, Rufus was attached to the retinue of the governor of Africa. Walking in a portico towards evening, a female figure of more than human size appeared to him and said she was Africa, and told him what was to come: he would go to Rome, hold office, return to that same province with the highest power, and there die. Everything happened as she had said. The story continues that as he was leaving the ship at Carthage the same figure met him on the shore. He certainly fell ill; and, judging the future by the past and misfortune by his prosperity, he abandoned hope of recovery even though none of his people despaired.
context: This is the most famous ghost letter in Latin literature and the ultimate source of the haunted-house story in the European tradition. Pliny frames it as a philosophical inquiry — an sint aliquid — addressed to Licinius Sura, a learned friend and confidant of Trajan, which is itself an epistolary convention: the letter poses a question in order to display the material.

lines.latin: Et mihi discendi et tibi docendi facultatem otium praebet. Igitur perquam velim scire, esse phantasmata et habere propriam figuram numenque aliquod putes an inania et vana ex metu nostro imaginem accipere.
lines.english: Leisure offers both to me the opportunity of learning and to you of teaching. Therefore I would very much like to know whether you think that ghosts exist and have their own shape and some divine power, or that, empty and vain, they receive an image from our fear.

lines.latin: Ego ut esse credam in primis eo ducor, quod audio accidisse Curtio Rufo. Tenuis adhuc et obscurus, obtinenti Africam comes haeserat. Inclinato die spatiabatur in porticu; offertur ei mulieris figura humana grandior pulchriorque. Perterrito Africam se futurorum praenuntiam dixit: iturum enim Romam honoresque gesturum, atque etiam cum summo imperio in eandem provinciam reversurum, ibique moriturum.
lines.english: I am led to believe that they exist especially by this, which I hear happened to Curtius Rufus. Still poor and unknown, he had attached himself as a companion to the man holding Africa. As the day was declining he was walking in a colonnade; there presents itself to him the figure of a woman, larger and more beautiful than human. To him, terrified, she said that she was Africa, foreteller of future things: for [she said] that he would go to Rome and would hold offices, and also would return to the same province with the highest command, and would die there.

lines.latin: Facta sunt omnia. Praeterea accedenti Carthaginem egredientique nave eadem figura in litore occurrisse narratur. Ipse certe implicitus morbo futura praeteritis, adversa secundis auguratus, spem salutis nullo suorum desperante proiecit.
lines.english: All things happened. Moreover, as he was approaching Carthage and disembarking from his ship, the same figure is said to have met [him] on the shore. He himself certainly, struck by disease, having foretold the future from the past, adversity from prosperity, threw away hope of recovery, although none of his people was despairing.

lines.latin: Iam illud nonne et magis terribile et non minus mirum est quod exponam ut accepi?
lines.english: Now is not that [story] both more terrifying and no less amazing which I will set forth as I received it?

lines.latin: Erat Athenis spatiosa et capax domus sed infamis et pestilens. Per silentium noctis sonus ferri, et si attenderes acrius, strepitus vinculorum longius primo, deinde e proximo reddebatur: mox apparebat idolon, senex macie et squalore confectus, promissa barba horrenti capillo; cruribus compedes, manibus catenas gerebat quatiebatque.
lines.english: There was at Athens a spacious and roomy house, but notorious and unhealthy. Through the silence of the night a sound of iron and, if you were paying attention more sharply, a clanking of chains was given back, at first rather far off, then from close by: soon there was appearing a phantom, an old man worn out with thinness and filth, with a long beard [and] bristling hair; he was wearing fetters on his legs, chains on his hands, and was shaking them.

lines.latin: Inde inhabitantibus tristes diraeque noctes per metum vigilabantur; vigiliam morbus et crescente formidine mors sequebatur. Nam interdiu quoque, quamquam abscesserat imago, memoria imaginis oculis inerrabat, longiorque causis timoris timor erat. Deserta inde et damnata solitudine domus totaque illi monstro relicta; proscribebatur tamen, seu quis emere seu quis conducere ignarus tanti mali vellet.
lines.english: Thence for the inhabitants sad and dreadful nights were spent awake through fear; disease followed wakefulness and, as the dread grew, death. For in the daytime too, although the image had gone away, the memory of the image was wandering before their eyes, and the fear was longer than the causes of fear. Thereafter the house [was] deserted and condemned to solitude and left entirely to that monster; it was advertised, however, in case anyone ignorant of so great an evil wanted to buy or to rent [it].

lines.latin: Venit Athenas philosophus Athenodorus, legit titulum auditoque pretio, quia suspecta vilitas, percunctatus omnia docetur ac nihilo minus, immo tanto magis conducit. Ubi coepit advesperascere, iubet sterni sibi in prima domus parte, poscit pugillares stilum lumen, suos omnes in interiora dimittit; ipse ad scribendum animum oculos manum intendit, ne vacua mens audita simulacra et inanes sibi metus fingeret.
lines.english: The philosopher Athenodorus comes to Athens, reads the notice and, the price having been heard, because the cheapness [was] suspicious, having inquired, he is told everything, and none the less, rather all the more, he rents [it]. When it began to grow dark, he orders [a couch] to be spread for himself in the front part of the house; he asks for writing tablets, a stylus, a light; he sends all his people away into the inner [rooms]; he himself directs his mind, eyes, hand to writing, so that his idle mind might not invent for itself phantoms heard about and empty fears.

lines.latin: Initio, quale ubique, silentium noctis; dein concuti ferrum, vincula moveri. Ille non tollere oculos, non remittere stilum, sed offirmare animum auribusque praetendere. Tum crebrescere fragor, adventare et iam ut in limine, iam ut intra limen audiri. Respicit, videt agnoscitque narratam sibi effigiem.
lines.english: At the beginning, as everywhere, the silence of the night; then iron [began] to be shaken, chains to be moved. He [did] not raise his eyes, not let go of his stylus, but strengthened his mind and held it out before his ears. Then the crash [began] to grow louder, to approach, and to be heard now as if on the threshold, now as if within the threshold. He looks back; he sees and recognizes the figure described to him.

author: pliny
title: Ghosts: Athenodorus Follows the Phantom
summary: Pliny turns to a more frightening story. There was a large and roomy house in Athens with an evil reputation: in the silence of the night a noise of iron and, if you listened closely, the clank of chains was heard, far off at first and then nearer; then a phantom appeared, an old man wasted and filthy, with a long beard and bristling hair, wearing fetters on his legs and chains on his hands and shaking them. The inhabitants passed dreadful, sleepless nights; illness and death followed, and the house stood empty and condemned to solitude, though it was advertised in case anyone unaware of the evil should wish to buy or rent it. The philosopher Athenodorus came, read the notice, and, when he heard the price, suspected something and became keener still on hearing the whole story. As evening came he had a couch laid out in the front part of the house and called for writing tablets, a pen and a lamp, sending all his household to the inner rooms and applying his mind, eyes and hand to writing so that his mind should not invent the phantoms he had heard of. At first there was only the silence of night, then the shaking of iron and the movement of chains; he did not look up or put down his pen but steadied his mind against the sound. The noise grew, came to the threshold, and entered. He looked, saw the shape as described, and it stood beckoning with a finger. He gestured for it to wait a little and bent again over his tablets; it rattled its chains over his head. He looked again and saw it beckoning as before, took up the lamp and followed. It moved slowly, weighed down by the chains, turned into the courtyard, and suddenly vanished, leaving him alone; he marked the place with grass and leaves. Next day he went to the magistrates and advised them to have the spot dug up: bones were found bound with chains, which the body, decayed by time and the soil, had left bare. They were collected and buried at public expense, and after the proper rites the house was troubled no more.
context: The Athenodorus story is the classic ancient haunted-house narrative and turns on a specifically Roman religious point: the ghost is restless because the corpse lacked proper burial, and the rite once performed lays it. Pliny's philosopher hero deliberately refuses to let his imagination create the ghost — the story is constructed to defeat the sceptical explanation before it is offered.

lines.latin: Stabat innuebatque digito similis vocanti. Hic contra ut paulum exspectaret manu significat rursusque ceris et stilo incumbit. Illa scribentis capiti catenis insonabat. Respicit rursus idem quod prius innuentem, nec moratus tollit lumen et sequitur.
lines.english: It was standing and beckoning with its finger, like one calling. He in turn signals with his hand that it wait a little, and again bends over his wax tablets and stylus. It was clanking with its chains over the head of [him] writing. He looks back again [at it], beckoning the same as before, and without delay he picks up the light and follows.

lines.latin: Ibat illa lento gradu quasi gravis vinculis. Postquam deflexit in aream domus, repente dilapsa deserit comitem. Desertus herbas et folia concerpta signum loco ponit.
lines.english: It was going with a slow step, as if heavy with chains. After it turned aside into the courtyard of the house, suddenly vanishing it deserts its companion. Deserted, he places plucked grass and leaves as a mark at the spot.

lines.latin: Postero die adit magistratus, monet ut illum locum effodi iubeant. Inveniuntur ossa inserta catenis et implicita, quae corpus aevo terraque putrefactum nuda et exesa reliquerat vinculis; collecta publice sepeliuntur. Domus postea rite conditis manibus caruit.
lines.english: On the next day he approaches the magistrates [and] advises that they order that place to be dug up. Bones are found, inserted into and entwined with chains, which the body, rotted by age and earth, had left bare and eaten away in the chains; collected, they are buried at public expense. Afterward, the spirits having been duly laid to rest, the house was free [of it].

lines.latin: Et haec quidem affirmantibus credo; illud affirmare aliis possum. Est libertus mihi non illitteratus. Cum hoc minor frater eodem lecto quiescebat. Is visus est sibi cernere quendam in toro residentem, admoventemque capiti suo cultros, atque etiam ex ipso vertice amputantem capillos. Ubi illuxit, ipse circa verticem tonsus, capilli iacentes reperiuntur.
lines.english: And these things indeed I believe on the word of those affirming them; that [next one] I can affirm to others. There is a freedman of mine, not unlettered. With him a younger brother was sleeping in the same bed. He seemed to himself to see someone sitting on the couch and moving knives to his head, and even cutting off hair from the very top [of his head]. When it grew light, he himself [was] shorn around the top, [and] the hair is found lying [there].

lines.latin: Exiguum temporis medium, et rursus simile aliud priori fidem fecit. Puer in paedagogio mixtus pluribus dormiebat. Venerunt per fenestras — ita narrat — in tunicis albis duo cubantemque detonderunt et qua venerant recesserunt. Hunc quoque tonsum sparsosque circa capillos dies ostendit.
lines.english: A short interval of time [passed], and again another similar [event] made the earlier believable. A slave boy was sleeping in the pages’ quarters, mixed with several [others]. There came through the windows — so he tells — two [figures] in white tunics, and they sheared him as he lay and went back the way they had come. Daylight showed this one too shorn and the hair scattered around.

lines.latin: Nihil notabile secutum, nisi forte quod non fui reus, futurus, si Domitianus sub quo haec acciderunt diutius vixisset. Nam in scrinio eius datus a Caro de me libellus inventus est; ex quo coniectari potest, quia reis moris est summittere capillum, recisos meorum capillos depulsi quod imminebat periculi signum fuisse.
lines.english: Nothing notable followed, unless perhaps that I was not a defendant, [as I] would have been if Domitian, under whom these things happened, had lived longer. For in his writing case was found a document about me given by Carus; from which it can be conjectured, because it is the custom for defendants to let their hair grow, that the cut hair of my [slaves] was a sign of the danger which was threatening having been driven away.

lines.latin: Proinde rogo, eruditionem tuam intendas. Digna res est quam diu multumque consideres; ne ego quidem indignus, cui copiam scientiae tuae facias.
lines.english: Therefore I ask that you apply your learning. The matter is worthy for you to consider long and much; not even I am unworthy, for whom you should make available the abundance of your knowledge.

lines.latin: Licet etiam utramque in partem — ut soles — disputes, ex altera tamen fortius, ne me suspensum incertumque dimittas, cum mihi consulendi causa fuerit, ut dubitare desinerem. Vale.
lines.english: You may even argue on both sides — as you usually do —, but more strongly on one, so that you do not send me away in suspense and uncertain, since for me the reason for consulting [you] was that I might stop doubting. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: Trajan's Reply on Harpocras
summary: Trajan replies that he has followed the practice of his predecessors in granting Alexandrian citizenship sparingly, but that since Pliny has already obtained Roman citizenship for his doctor Harpocras he cannot refuse this request either. He tells Pliny to write to him which prefecture Harpocras belongs to, so that he may send a letter to his friend Pompeius Planta, prefect of Egypt.
context: Trajan's replies are markedly short, plain and businesslike beside Pliny's elaborate requests, and the contrast in style is itself a standard subject for AP style-and-context questions. Note that this letter carries the heading TRAIANUS PLINIO, not C. PLINIUS TRAIANO.

lines.latin: Civitatem Alexandrinam secundum institutionem principum non temere dare proposui. Sed cum Arpocrati, iatraliptae tuo, iam civitatem Romanam impetraveris, huic quoque petitioni tuae negare non sustineo. Tu, ex quo nomo sit, notum mihi facere debebis, ut epistulam tibi ad Pompeium Plantam praefectum Aegypti amicum meum mittam.
lines.english: I have resolved, in accordance with the practice of the emperors, not to give Alexandrian citizenship rashly. But since you have already obtained Roman citizenship for Harpocras, your masseur, I cannot bring myself to refuse this petition of yours too. You will have to make known to me from which district he is, so that I may send you a letter to my friend Pompeius Planta, prefect of Egypt.

author: pliny
title: To Trajan: Citizenship for Harpocras
summary: Pliny tells Trajan that last year, when he was gravely ill and in danger of his life, he took on a masseur-doctor (iatraliptes), whose care and devotion he can repay only through the emperor's kindness. He therefore asks Roman citizenship for the man: Harpocras is of foreign status, freed by a foreign woman, Thermuthis daughter of Theon, who died long ago. He also asks the ius Quiritium for two freedwomen of Antonia Maximilla, a lady of distinction, at their patroness's own request.
context: Book 10 preserves Pliny's official correspondence with Trajan, unique in Latin literature for including the emperor's own replies. This exchange shows the mechanics of imperial patronage and the legal oddity that an Egyptian had to acquire Alexandrian citizenship before Roman citizenship. Note the formal address C. PLINIUS TRAIANO IMPERATORI.

lines.latin: Proximo anno, domine, gravissima valetudine usque ad periculum vitae vexatus iatralipten assumpsi; cuius sollicitudini et studio tuae tantum indulgentiae beneficio referre gratiam parem possum.
lines.english: Last year, lord, troubled by a very serious illness right up to the danger of my life, I took on a masseur, to whose care and zeal I can return equal thanks only by the favor of your indulgence.

lines.latin: Quare rogo des ei civitatem Romanam. Est enim peregrinae condicionis manumissus a peregrina. Vocatur ipse Arpocras, patronam habuit Thermuthin Theonis, quae iam pridem defuncta est. Item rogo des ius Quiritium libertis Antoniae Maximillae, ornatissimae feminae, Hediae et Antoniae Harmeridi; quod a te petente patrona peto.
lines.english: Therefore I ask that you give him Roman citizenship. For he is of foreign status, freed by a foreign woman. He himself is called Harpocras; he had as patroness Thermuthis, [daughter] of Theon, who died long ago. Likewise I ask that you give the right of the Quirites to the freedwomen of Antonia Maximilla, a most distinguished woman, Hedia and Antonia Harmeris; which I ask of you at the request of their patroness.

author: pliny
title: To Trajan: Thanks and a Further Request
summary: Pliny thanks Trajan for granting without delay both the ius Quiritium to the freedwomen of a lady close to him and Roman citizenship to his doctor Harpocras. But when he submitted the man's age and property, as Trajan had instructed, those more experienced told him he ought first to have obtained Alexandrian citizenship for him, and then Roman, since Harpocras was an Egyptian. Thinking Egyptians no different from other foreigners, he had written only that the man was freed by a foreign woman who had long since died. He does not complain of his ignorance, since it has left him obliged to Trajan more than once for the same man, and asks him to grant Alexandrian citizenship as well, so that he may enjoy the favor lawfully. He has sent the age and property to Trajan's freedmen, so that nothing should delay the emperor's kindness again.
context: The letter records Pliny getting the procedure wrong and having to ask again — a rare and humanising glimpse of provincial administration. It also shows Pliny's carefully deferential register when writing to the emperor, quite different from his tone to literary friends.

lines.latin: Ago gratias, domine, quod et ius Quiritium libertis necessariae mihi feminae et civitatem Romanam Arpocrati, iatraliptae meo, sine mora indulsisti. Sed cum annos eius et censum sicut praeceperas ederem, admonitus sum a peritioribus debuisse me ante ei Alexandrinam civitatem impetrare, deinde Romanam, quoniam esset Aegyptius.
lines.english: I give thanks, lord, because without delay you granted both the right of the Quirites to the freedwomen of a woman close to me and Roman citizenship to Harpocras, my masseur. But when I was submitting his age and property, as you had instructed, I was advised by those more experienced that I ought first to have obtained Alexandrian citizenship for him, then Roman, since he was an Egyptian.

lines.latin: Ego autem, quia inter Aegyptios ceterosque peregrinos nihil interesse credebam, contentus fueram hoc solum scribere tibi, esse eum a peregrina manumissum patronamque eius iam pridem decessisse. De qua ignorantia mea non queror, per quam stetit ut tibi pro eodem homine saepius obligarer. Rogo itaque, ut beneficio tuo legitime frui possim, tribuas ei et Alexandrinam civitatem [et Romanam]. Annos eius et censum, ne quid rursus indulgentiam tuam moraretur, libertis tuis quibus iusseras misi.
lines.english: I, however, because I believed that there was no difference between Egyptians and other foreigners, had been content to write to you only this, that he had been freed by a foreign woman and that his patroness had died long ago. About this ignorance of mine I do not complain, through which it came about that I was obliged to you more than once for the same man. I ask therefore that, so that I may lawfully enjoy your favor, you grant him both Alexandrian citizenship [and Roman]. His age and property, so that nothing might again delay your indulgence, I have sent to your freedmen, to whom you had ordered [them sent].

author: pliny
title: To Trajan: The Aqueduct at Nicomedia
summary: Pliny reports that the people of Nicomedia have spent 3,318,000 sesterces on an aqueduct which was abandoned unfinished and then demolished; then a further 200,000 was granted for another, which was also abandoned, so that a new outlay is needed for those who have wasted so much money to have water. He has himself visited a very pure spring from which it seems water should be brought, as was attempted at the start, by an arched structure, so that it may reach not only the low and level parts of the city. A very few arches still survive, and others can be built from the squared stone taken from the earlier work; part, he thinks, should be made of brick, which is easier and cheaper. But first Trajan must send an engineer or an architect to prevent what happened before, since he can guarantee that the project is worthy of the emperor's reign in both utility and beauty.
context: The clearest surviving picture of Roman provincial public works and of an emperor's direct oversight of them. Pliny was sent to Bithynia-Pontus around 110 CE precisely because the province's finances were mismanaged; the aqueduct letters show that brief in action.

author: pliny
title: To Trajan: Water for Sinope
summary: Pliny reports that the citizens of Sinope lack water, but that good and abundant water can be brought from the sixteenth milestone, though there is a doubtful and soft stretch of ground just over a mile from the source. He has meanwhile ordered it to be explored at small expense to see whether it can carry the weight of a structure. Money will not be lacking, provided that Trajan supports a work so conducive to the health and pleasure of a very thirsty colony.
context: A companion to 10.37, and a good example of Pliny's habitual method: investigate first, cost it, then request imperial approval. Trajan's reply (10.91) grants it, on condition the city can pay.

lines.english: The people of Sinope, lord, lack water, which seems able to be brought, both good and plentiful, from the sixteenth milestone. There is, however, right at the source, a little more than a mile [along], a suspect and soft place, which I have meanwhile ordered to be explored at moderate expense, [to see] whether it can receive and support the work.

lines.english: Money, collected through our care, will not be lacking, if you, lord, grant this kind of work both to the health and to the pleasantness of a very thirsty colony.

author: vergil
title: The Epic Begins
summary: Vergil states his theme — arms and the man — and traces Aeneas' journey from Troy to Italy, driven by fate and hounded by Juno's remembered anger. He invokes the Muse to explain why a goddess would drive so pious a man through so much suffering, then sets out Juno's motives: her love for Carthage, which fate has doomed to fall to a Trojan race, and her memory of the Judgement of Paris and the rape of Ganymede.
context: The proem establishes the Aeneid as a Roman answer to Homer: arma echoes the Iliad, virum the Odyssey. The programmatic first word arma and the phrase Troiae qui primus ab oris announce a foundation epic that culminates in Augustan Rome. Tantaene animis caelestibus irae? (1.11) frames the poem's central theological problem.

author: vergil
title: The Storm
summary: Aeolus releases the winds at Juno's request and a violent storm falls on the Trojan fleet. Darkness covers the sky, thunder flashes, and the men face immediate death. Aeneas, unmanned by cold fear, stretches his hands to the stars and cries out that those who died at Troy before their fathers' eyes were three and four times blessed. The storm smashes the ships; one is driven under by a towering wave.
context: The storm is modelled on Odyssey 5, but Aeneas' first words in the poem are a wish that he had died at Troy — a striking departure from Odysseus' resourcefulness, and central to debates about Aeneas as a hero. Note extemplo Aeneae solvuntur frigore membra (1.92), a line Vergil reuses of Turnus at the poem's end (12.951).

author: vergil
title: Queen Dido
summary: Dido comes to the temple surrounded by a great throng of young men. Vergil compares her to Diana leading her dancing bands along the banks of the Eurotas or over Cynthus, with a thousand mountain nymphs thronging about her, as Latona's heart silently rejoices. Dido bears herself among her people, urging on the work of her rising kingdom, and takes her seat on a high throne in the temple doorway, hedged by armed men.
context: Dido's introduction through a Diana simile answers the Nausicaa simile of Odyssey 6, and marks her as a legitimate, virginal ruler — which makes her later fall the more tragic. The simile is also a subtle warning: Diana is the goddess who destroys those who violate her.

author: vergil
title: Laocoön Warns the Trojans
summary: Laocoön runs down from the citadel and rebukes the Trojans for believing the Greeks have gone: either Achaeans are hidden in the horse, or it is an engine built against their walls. He warns them not to trust it — whatever it is, he fears the Greeks even when they bring gifts — and hurls his spear into the horse's flank, which groans. Vergil comments that, had the gods and Trojan minds not been against it, Laocoön would have made them destroy the horse, and Troy would still stand.

author: vergil
title: The Death of Laocoön
summary: Laocoön, chosen priest of Neptune, is sacrificing a bull when two serpents come over the calm sea from Tenedos, their blood-red crests above the waves. They make straight for him, first seizing and devouring his two young sons, then binding Laocoön himself as he tries to help; he roars like a wounded bull. The serpents escape to the citadel of Tritonian Minerva. The Trojans read the death as punishment for wounding the horse and breach their own walls to drag it into the city, while Cassandra's prophecies go unheeded.
context: The Laocoön episode is the subject of the famous Hellenistic sculpture group in the Vatican. Vergil's serpents are described with intensely visual and aural effects — note the alliteration and sibilance. The Trojans' misreading of an unambiguous portent is the hinge on which Troy falls.

author: vergil
title: Dido Feels the Effect of Cupid
summary: Dido leads Aeneas through the city, showing him Sidonian wealth and the city she has founded; she begins to speak and stops half-way. As day fades she seeks the same banquet again, madly asks again to hear the Trojan sufferings, and hangs again on the speaker's lips. When the guests have gone and the moon is dimming, she grieves alone in the empty hall and lies on the couch he has left, hearing and seeing him though he is absent. She holds Ascanius in her lap, beguiled by his likeness to his father. The towers stop rising, the young men cease their drill, the harbours and battlements stand unfinished.
context: Vergil presents love as a disease and a wound (uritur infelix Dido). The collapse of Carthaginian building work is a political consequence of private passion — a theme with obvious Augustan resonance, and the mirror image of Aeneas' own duty to found a city.

author: vergil
title: The Cave and Rumor
summary: Dido and the Trojan leader come to the same cave; earth and Juno give the sign, lightning flashes, and the nymphs cry out on the mountain top. That day was the first cause of death and of disaster; Dido calls it a marriage and screens her fault with that name. At once Rumor goes through the great cities of Libya — an evil swifter than any other, growing as she goes, small at first through fear, then rising into the air with her head in the clouds. Vergil describes her as a monster with as many watchful eyes, tongues, mouths and pricked-up ears as she has feathers, flying by night and shrieking by day, clinging to lies and wrong as much as reporting truth. She fills the peoples with her tales, singing alike of what is done and not done.
context: The Fama passage is the most celebrated personification in Latin poetry, drawing on Hesiod and Homer but far exceeding them. Note coniugium vocat, hoc praetexit nomine culpam (4.172) — Vergil marks Dido's self-deception in a single line. The passage supplies the mechanism by which Iarbas, and then Jupiter, learn of the affair.

author: vergil
title: Aeneas Leaves Dido
summary: Dido confronts Aeneas: did he hope to conceal so great a wrong and leave her land in silence? She appeals to their love and her given right hand, to the death she will die, and asks him to pity a falling house; because of him the Libyan tribes and Nomad kings hate her, her own Tyrians are hostile, her honour is destroyed. She asks for whom she is being left, and calls him not even a guest but an enemy. Aeneas, holding his eyes fixed by Jupiter's warning, struggles to master his pain and answers briefly: he will never deny her kindnesses, nor regret remembering Elissa; he did not come as a suitor and never held out a marriage torch. If the fates allowed him to live as he chose he would be rebuilding Troy for his own people, but Grynean Apollo and the Lycian oracles order him to Italy — that is his love, that his country. He is driven too by the shade of his father Anchises and by concern for Ascanius' inheritance; Jupiter's own messenger has come to him. He ends: Italiam non sponte sequor.
context: The central confrontation of the poem, and the clearest collision between private feeling and public duty. Aeneas' speech has been read both as callous and as agonised; his opening desine meque tuis incendere teque querelis and closing Italiam non sponte sequor (4.361) are the key evidence for either case. Compare the Roman ideal of pietas against the Hellenistic ideal of erotic loyalty.

author: vergil
title: The Shade of Dido
summary: Among the shades in the Fields of Mourning Aeneas sees Phoenician Dido, her wound still fresh. He recognises her dimly through the shadows, as one who sees or thinks he has seen the moon rising through clouds at the month's beginning, and speaks to her in tears with sweet love: so the news was true that she had died by the sword. Was he the cause of her death? He swears by the stars, by the gods and by whatever faith there is beneath the earth that he left her shore unwillingly, and that he could not have believed his going would bring her such grief. He begs her to stop and not withdraw from his sight. Dido, hostile, keeps her eyes fixed on the ground, no more moved by his speech than if she were hard flint or Marpesian rock, and at last tears herself away into the shadowy grove where her first husband Sychaeus answers her love.
context: Dido's silence is one of the most admired effects in ancient literature — Vergil gives the poem's most eloquent speaker no words at all. Invitus, regina, tuo de litore cessi (6.460) deliberately echoes Catullus 66. The reunion with Sychaeus restores what Book 4 destroyed.

author: vergil
title: The Parade of Heroes: Augustus
summary: Anchises points out Caesar and the whole line of Iulus destined to come beneath the great vault of heaven. Here is the man so often promised to Aeneas, Augustus Caesar, son of a god, who will found the golden age again in Latium through the fields once ruled by Saturn, and extend the empire beyond the Garamantes and the Indians, to a land beyond the stars, beyond the paths of the year and the sun, where sky-bearing Atlas turns the vault studded with burning constellations. Already now the Caspian realms and the Maeotian land shudder at his coming, and the mouths of the sevenfold Nile are troubled.
context: The most explicitly Augustan passage in the poem. Divi genus (6.792) refers to Augustus as son of the deified Julius Caesar. The claim that he will extend empire beyond the sun's path is imperial panegyric of a very high order, and is often set against the poem's darker closing.

author: vergil
title: The Arts of Rome
summary: Anchises concedes that others will hammer out breathing bronze more finely and draw living faces from marble, plead cases better, trace the movements of the heavens with the rod and predict the rising stars. But the Roman is to remember to rule the peoples with power — these will be his arts — to impose the custom of peace, to spare the conquered and to war down the proud.
context: Tu regere imperio populos, Romane, memento (6.851) is the programmatic statement of Rome's imperial mission and the most quoted passage of Book 6. Parcere subiectis et debellare superbos supplies the standard against which the poem's own ending — Aeneas killing a suppliant Turnus — is measured.

author: vergil
title: King Latinus
summary: Vergil announces a greater order of things and a greater work. King Latinus, now old, was ruling the fields and towns in long-settled peace. He was born, we are told, of Faunus and the Laurentine nymph Marica; Picus was Faunus' father, and Picus claims Saturn as his ultimate ancestor. By the gods' decree Latinus had no son — his only boy was taken in early youth — and a single daughter kept the great house, now ripe for a husband and of full marriageable age. Many sought her from great Latium and all Ausonia; handsomest of them all was Turnus, powerful in ancestry, whom the queen longed to join to her as son-in-law — but divine portents stood in the way.
context: Maius opus moveo (7.45) marks the start of the poem's 'Iliadic' second half. The genealogy grounds Latinus in Italian and Saturnian tradition, making the coming war a civil conflict among kin, which sharpens its Roman resonance.

author: vergil
title: Turnus Prepares for War
summary: Turnus moves among the front ranks, outstanding in body and a whole head taller than the rest. His tall helmet, crested with three plumes, carries a Chimaera breathing Etnean fires from its jaws — raging the more fiercely with sad flames the more the fighting grows bloody. On his polished shield Io is emblazoned in gold with lifted horns, already covered with bristles and already a heifer — a great device — and Argus her guardian, and her father Inachus pouring his stream from an engraved urn.
context: The arming of Turnus is a set piece with Homeric precedent. Both devices are ominous: the Chimaera was killed by Bellerophon, and Io was a victim of Juno's jealousy — emblems that align Turnus with Juno's cause and hint at his defeat.

author: vergil
title: Camilla Introduced
summary: Last comes Camilla of the Volscian people, leading a column of cavalry and squadrons flowering in bronze — a warrior woman whose hands were never trained to Minerva's distaff or workbaskets, but a maiden hardened to endure battle and to outstrip the winds in running. She could have flown over the topmost blades of unmown corn without bruising the tender ears, or held her way over the swell of the mid-sea without dipping her swift soles in the water. All the young men pouring from house and field, and crowds of mothers, marvel at her as she goes and watch open-mouthed, at the royal purple draping her smooth shoulders, the clasp entwining her hair in gold, and the way she carries her Lycian quiver and shepherd's myrtle staff tipped with a spear point.
context: Camilla closes the catalogue of Italian forces, in the position Homer gives to the most striking figure. The adynaton-like simile of her speed is one of Vergil's most admired. She belongs to a tradition of warrior maidens — Penthesilea, the Amazons — and her Book 11 aristeia and death are required reading.

author: vergil
title: The Story of Camilla
summary: Diana speaks to the nymph Opis, telling her that Camilla goes to a war she cannot win and that she has long loved her above all others. Camilla's father Metabus, driven from Privernum by hatred and civil war, carried the infant with him into exile. Fleeing with the Volscians in pursuit he reached the flooded river Amasenus; unable to swim while carrying the child, he bound her to a great spear, prayed to Diana, vowing the girl to her as her servant, hurled the spear with its burden across the roaring water and swam after it under a shower of weapons. He raised her in lonely mountains and woods on the milk of a wild mare, dressed her in a tiger skin, gave her a javelin and bow instead of a girl's toys, and refused every marriage offer; she remained content with Diana alone, cherishing an unbroken love of her weapons and of virginity. Diana ends by ordering Opis to descend, guard Camilla, and take vengeance on whoever wounds her.
context: The story is told as a divine flashback, giving Camilla a full tragic biography before her aristeia and death later in the book. The spear-throw across the Amasenus is Vergil's own invention and one of his most memorable scenes. Camilla's consecration to Diana connects her to Dido's Diana simile in Book 1.

author: vergil
title: Jupiter Speaks to Juno
summary: The king of high Olympus addresses Juno, who is watching the battle from a golden cloud: what will the end be? What is left at the last? Aeneas is owed to heaven as a native god, and the fates will raise him to the stars — she knows and admits she knows it. What is she contriving, and with what hope does she cling to the cold clouds?
context: The opening of the divine reconciliation that settles the poem. Jupiter's question quae iam finis erit, coniunx? answers the poem's opening question about the anger of the gods (1.11).

title: Juno Yields
summary: Jupiter forbids Juno to go further: he has been able to drive her from earth and sea and to raise storms, and to debase Turnus, but she must desist. Juno, with lowered gaze, replies that it was because she knew that will of his that she left Turnus and the earth against her wishes; otherwise Jupiter would not see her enduring insults alone, girt with flame in the front line and dragging the Trojans into hostile battle. She admits she urged Juturna to help her unhappy brother and approved her daring greater things for his life — but not that she should aim arrows or draw the bow.
context: Juno's climb-down is grudging and partial, and Vergil marks it with demisso lumine. This is the resolution of the wrath announced in the proem, but it is achieved by bargain, not by conversion.

author: vergil
title: Juno's Terms
summary: Juno makes her request, which she says no law of fate forbids: for the sake of Latium and the greatness of Jupiter's own people, when the two sides make peace by a happy marriage, let him not order the native Latins to change their ancient name, to become Trojans or to be called Teucrians; let the men not change their speech or their dress. Let Latium endure, let there be Alban kings through the ages, let the Roman stock be strong through Italian valour — Troy has fallen, and let it have fallen along with its name.
context: This is the ideological settlement of the whole poem: Rome is to be Italian in language, dress and name, with a Trojan dynasty. Occidit, occideritque sinas cum nomine Troia (12.828) is Vergil's resolution of the tension between Trojan origin and Roman identity, and a passage of obvious Augustan significance.

author: vergil
title: The Final Battle of Aeneas and Turnus
summary: Aeneas hurls his spear like a black whirlwind; it pierces the rim of Turnus' shield and lodges in his thigh, and huge Turnus sinks to the ground with his knee doubled under him. The Rutulians rise with a groan and the whole mountain range echoes. Turnus, humbled, stretches out his hand as a suppliant and says he has deserved it and does not beg; Aeneas should use his luck. But if any care for a parent can touch him, he begs him to pity old Daunus — as Anchises was to Aeneas — and to return him, or his body, to his people. He acknowledges Aeneas has won and that the Ausonians have seen him stretch out his hands; Lavinia is his wife, and he should not press his hatred further. Aeneas stands fierce in his arms and holds back his hand, and the words were beginning to sway him more and more, when high on Turnus' shoulder the unlucky baldric of the boy Pallas appears with its familiar studs. Blazing with fury and terrible in his anger, Aeneas cries that Turnus, wearing the spoils of his own, shall not be snatched from him: it is Pallas who sacrifices him and exacts the penalty from his guilty blood. Saying this he buries the sword full in Turnus' breast; his limbs go slack with cold, and his life flees with a groan, resentful, to the shades below.
context: The most debated ending in classical literature. Aeneas hesitates — and then kills a suppliant in fury, an act measured against Anchises' parcere subiectis (6.853). Note that vitaque cum gemitu fugit indignata sub umbras repeats the line used of Camilla's death (11.831), and that Aeneas' furiis accensus et ira echoes the poem's opening account of Juno's saevae memorem iram.
