author: caesar
title: The Three Parts of Gaul
summary: Caesar opens his commentary with a geographic and ethnographic survey: Gaul is divided into three parts, inhabited respectively by the Belgae, the Aquitani, and the Celts (called Galli by the Romans), each differing in language, institutions, and law. Three rivers mark the boundaries between them. The Belgae are judged the bravest, because they are farthest from the civilizing (and, in Caesar's telling, softening) influence of the Roman province and are in constant contact and conflict with the Germans across the Rhine — the same proximity to Germanic warfare that makes the Helvetii the most warlike of the Gauls proper. The chapter closes by locating each of the three regions relative to the Rhone, the Rhine, the Pyrenees, and the Ocean.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — the syllabus is fixed to Vergil and Pliny — but placed here in Unit 1 ("Teacher's Choice — Latin Prose") because no other opening of a Latin prose work is better known or more often excerpted for beginning students. Caesar wrote his own military and political record in the third person, styling it commentarii ("notes, memoranda") rather than history proper — a pose of plain, unadorned factual reporting that is itself a rhetorical choice, not a neutral one. The ethnographic framing here (praising the Belgae and Helvetii for their remoteness from "civilizing" contact) also does real political work: it justifies the nine-year war of conquest that follows as a response to a genuinely dangerous frontier, not naked expansion.

lines.latin: Gallia est omnis divisa in partes tres, quarum unam incolunt Belgae, aliam Aquitani, tertiam qui ipsorum lingua Celtae, nostra Galli appellantur.
lines.english: Gaul as a whole is divided into three parts, of which the Belgae inhabit one, the Aquitani another, [and] those who are called Celts in their own language, Gauls in ours, the third.

lines.latin: Hi omnes lingua, institutis, legibus inter se differunt.
lines.english: These all differ among themselves in language, institutions, [and] laws.

lines.latin: Gallos ab Aquitanis Garumna flumen, a Belgis Matrona et Sequana dividit.
lines.english: The river Garonne divides the Gauls from the Aquitani, the Marne and the Seine [divide them] from the Belgae.

lines.latin: Horum omnium fortissimi sunt Belgae, propterea quod a cultu atque humanitate provinciae longissime absunt, minimeque ad eos mercatores saepe commeant atque ea quae ad effeminandos animos pertinent important, proximique sunt Germanis, qui trans Rhenum incolunt, quibuscum continenter bellum gerunt.
lines.english: Of all these the bravest are the Belgae, because they are farthest away from the culture and refinement of the Province, and merchants least often travel to them and bring in those things which tend toward weakening minds, and they are nearest to the Germans, who live across the Rhine, with whom they continually wage war.

lines.latin: Qua de causa Helvetii quoque reliquos Gallos virtute praecedunt, quod fere cotidianis proeliis cum Germanis contendunt, cum aut suis finibus eos prohibent aut ipsi in eorum finibus bellum gerunt.
lines.english: For this reason the Helvetii also surpass the rest of the Gauls in courage, because they contend with the Germans in almost daily battles, when either they keep them from their own territory or they themselves wage war in their territory.

lines.latin: Eorum una pars, quam Gallos obtinere dictum est, initium capit a flumine Rhodano, continetur Garumna flumine, Oceano, finibus Belgarum, attingit etiam ab Sequanis et Helvetiis flumen Rhenum, vergit ad septentriones.
lines.english: One part of these, which it has been said the Gauls occupy, takes its beginning from the river Rhone; it is bounded by the river Garonne, the Ocean, [and] the territory of the Belgae; it also touches, on the side of the Sequani and the Helvetii, the river Rhine; it slopes toward the north.

lines.latin: Belgae ab extremis Galliae finibus oriuntur, pertinent ad inferiorem partem fluminis Rheni, spectant in septentrionem et orientem solem.
lines.english: The Belgae rise from the farthest borders of Gaul, extend to the lower part of the river Rhine, [and] look toward the north and the rising sun.

lines.latin: Aquitania a Garumna flumine ad Pyrenaeos montes et eam partem Oceani quae est ad Hispaniam pertinet; spectat inter occasum solis et septentriones.
lines.english: Aquitania extends from the river Garonne to the Pyrenees mountains and that part of the Ocean which is near Spain; it looks between the setting of the sun and the north.

author: pliny
salutation: C. PLINIUS CORNELIO TACITO SUO S.
title: Hunting with a Notebook
summary: Pliny tells Tacitus he will laugh, and he may: Pliny, that very man Tacitus knows, has caught three boars, and very fine ones. He himself? Yes — though without entirely abandoning his own idleness and quiet. He was sitting by the nets; there was no hunting spear or lance beside him but a stylus and writing tablets. He was thinking something over and making notes, so that even if he came back with empty hands he would have full tablets. That way of study should not be despised: it is remarkable how the mind is roused by the movement and exercise of the body. The woods all round, the solitude and the very silence that hunting demands are great stimulants to thought. So when Tacitus hunts, he should take along a lunch basket and a flask — and his tablets too; he will find that Minerva wanders in the mountains no less than Diana.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — included here as supplementary reading. It is one of Pliny's most quoted letters, and a good short prose piece for sight practice, with a neatly turned closing epigram on Minerva and Diana.

lines.latin: Ridebis, et licet rideas. Ego, ille quem nosti, apros tres et quidem pulcherrimos cepi. 'Ipse?' inquis. Ipse; non tamen ut omnino ab inertia mea et quiete discederem. Ad retia sedebam; erat in proximo non venabulum aut lancea, sed stilus et pugillares; meditabar aliquid enotabamque, ut si manus vacuas, plenas tamen ceras reportarem.
lines.english: You will laugh, and you may laugh. I, that [man] whom you know, have caught three boars, and indeed very beautiful ones. “You yourself?” you say. [I] myself; not, however, so that I departed altogether from my inactivity and quiet. I was sitting by the nets; there was nearby not a hunting spear or a lance, but a stylus and writing tablets; I was thinking something over and noting it down, so that, if [I brought back] empty hands, I might nevertheless bring back full wax tablets.

lines.latin: Non est quod contemnas hoc studendi genus; mirum est ut animus agitatione motuque corporis excitetur; iam undique silvae et solitudo ipsumque illud silentium quod venationi datur, magna cogitationis incitamenta sunt.
lines.english: There is no reason for you to despise this kind of studying; it is wonderful how the mind is aroused by the activity and motion of the body; besides, the woods on every side and the solitude and that very silence which is given to hunting are great incentives to thought.

lines.latin: Proinde cum venabere, licebit auctore me ut panarium et lagunculam sic etiam pugillares feras: experieris non Dianam magis montibus quam Minervam inerrare. Vale.
lines.english: Therefore, when you hunt, it will be permitted, on my authority, to carry writing tablets just as [you carry] a bread basket and a little flask: you will find that Minerva wanders the mountains no less than Diana. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: A Dinner Party and Social Rank
summary: Pliny describes dining with a man who thought his arrangement elegant and economical but who seemed to Pliny extravagant and mean at once: the best food was set before himself and a few others, cheap scraps before the rest, and even the wine was divided into three kinds — one for himself and Pliny, one for lesser friends, and one for his own and Pliny's freedmen. A fellow guest asked whether Pliny approved; he said no. Asked what his own practice was, he answered that he sets the same before everyone, since he invites people to dinner, not to a grading, and makes equal in every respect those he has made equal by his invitation — including freedmen, whom he then regards as fellow diners. His companion asked whether that was not expensive; not at all, Pliny replies, because his freedmen do not drink what he drinks — he drinks what they do. Anyone who moderates his own appetite will find it no burden to share what he has with many. That appetite is what should be restrained and brought to heel if one wishes to spare expense — better served by one's own self-control than by insults to others.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary. A famous letter on Roman dining etiquette, freedmen, and social hierarchy, and a valuable companion to the required letters for questions about Roman social relationships.

lines.latin: Longum est altius repetere nec refert, quemadmodum acciderit, ut homo minime familiaris cenarem apud quendam, ut sibi videbatur, lautum et diligentem, ut mihi, sordidum simul et sumptuosum.
lines.english: It is long to go back further, and it does not matter, how it happened that I, a man hardly a close friend, was dining at the house of a certain man, elegant and careful, as it seemed to himself, [but], as [it seemed] to me, at the same time stingy and extravagant.

lines.latin: Nam sibi et paucis opima quaedam, ceteris vilia et minuta ponebat. Vinum etiam parvolis lagunculis in tria genera discripserat, non ut potestas eligendi, sed ne ius esset recusandi, aliud sibi et nobis, aliud minoribus amicis - nam gradatim amicos habet -, aliud suis nostrisque libertis.
lines.english: For to himself and a few he was serving certain rich things, to the rest cheap and scanty things. He had even divided the wine in little flasks into three kinds, not so that there might be the power of choosing, but so that there might not be the right of refusing: one for himself and for us, another for the lesser friends — for he has friends by grades —, another for his and our freedmen.

lines.latin: Animadvertit qui mihi proximus recumbebat, et an probarem interrogavit. Negavi. 'Tu ergo' inquit 'quam consuetudinem sequeris?' 'Eadem omnibus pono; ad cenam enim, non ad notam invito cunctisque rebus exaequo, quos mensa et toro aequavi.'
lines.english: The man who was reclining next to me noticed, and asked whether I approved. I said no. “What custom, then,” he said, “do you follow?” “I serve the same things to all; for I invite [them] to dinner, not to a mark of disgrace, and I make equal in all things those whom I have made equal by table and couch.”

lines.latin: 'Etiamne libertos?' 'Etiam; convictores enim tunc, non libertos puto.' Et ille: 'Magno tibi constat.' 'Minime.' 'Qui fieri potest?' 'Quia scilicet liberti mei non idem quod ego bibunt, sed idem ego quod liberti.'
lines.english: “Even the freedmen?” “Even [them]; for I consider them then fellow diners, not freedmen.” And he: “It costs you a great deal.” “Not at all.” “How can it happen?” “Because, of course, my freedmen do not drink the same as I, but I [drink] the same as the freedmen.”

lines.latin: Et hercule si gulae temperes, non est onerosum quo utaris ipse communicare cum pluribus. Illa ergo reprimenda, illa quasi in ordinem redigenda est, si sumptibus parcas, quibus aliquanto rectius tua continentia quam aliena contumelia consulas.
lines.english: And, by Hercules, if you restrain your gluttony, it is not burdensome to share with many what you yourself use. That, therefore, must be held back, that must be brought back, as it were, into line, if you would spare expenses, for which you may provide rather more rightly by your own restraint than by insult to others.

lines.latin: Quorsus haec? ne tibi, optimae indolis iuveni, quorundam in mensa luxuria specie frugalitatis imponat. Convenit autem amori in te meo, quotiens tale aliquid inciderit, sub exemplo praemonere, quid debeas fugere.
lines.english: To what end [do I say] these things? So that the luxury of certain men at table, under the appearance of thrift, may not deceive you, a young man of excellent character. It suits my love for you, moreover, whenever some such thing has happened, to warn you in advance, by way of example, what you ought to avoid.

lines.latin: Igitur memento nihil magis esse vitandum quam istam luxuriae et sordium novam societatem; quae cum sint turpissima discreta ac separata, turpius iunguntur. Vale.
lines.english: Remember, therefore, that nothing is more to be avoided than that new partnership of luxury and meanness; which, although they are most shameful when distinct and separated, are joined more shamefully. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: To Calpurnia: Sleepless Nights
summary: Pliny writes that it is incredible how much he longs for Calpurnia. The cause is love first of all, and then that they are not used to being apart. So he spends the greater part of the night awake with her image; so by day, at the hours when he used to visit her, his feet carry him of their own accord to her rooms; so, finding them empty, he leaves, as sick and sorrowful as a shut-out lover from an unwelcoming doorway. The only time free from these torments is the time he wears out in the forum and in his friends' lawsuits. He asks her to judge what his life is like, when he finds rest in work and solace in troubles and anxieties.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary, though it is a natural companion to the required 6.4 and 6.7. The image of the shut-out lover (exclusus amator) is drawn straight from Latin love elegy, which is worth noting for style questions.

lines.latin: Incredibile est quanto desiderio tui tenear. In causa amor primum, deinde quod non consuevimus abesse. Inde est quod magnam noctium partem in imagine tua vigil exigo; inde quod interdiu, quibus horis te visere solebam, ad diaetam tuam ipsi me, ut verissime dicitur, pedes ducunt; quod denique aeger et maestus ac similis excluso a vacuo limine recedo. Unum tempus his tormentis caret, quo in foro et amicorum litibus conteror.
lines.english: It is unbelievable by how great a longing for you I am held. The cause is love first, then that we are not accustomed to be apart. Hence it is that I spend a great part of the nights awake with your image; hence that by day, at the hours at which I used to visit you, my feet themselves lead me, as is said most truly, to your room; that, finally, sick and sad and like one shut out, I withdraw from the empty threshold. One time is free of these torments, [the time] in which I am worn out in the forum and in the lawsuits of friends.

lines.latin: Aestima tu, quae vita mea sit, cui requies in labore, in miseria curisque solacium. Vale.
lines.english: You judge what my life is, for whom there is rest in toil, [and] comfort in misery and cares. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: Ummidia Quadratilla and Her Pantomimes
summary: Pliny reports the death of Ummidia Quadratilla just short of eighty, vigorous to her last illness and physically sturdy beyond the usual for a matron. She died leaving a very proper will, two thirds to her grandson and a third to her granddaughter. Pliny knew the granddaughter little; the grandson Quadratus he counts among his closest friends. He was a remarkable young man in a household hardly conducive to virtue: his grandmother kept a troupe of pantomime actors and indulged them more than suited a lady of rank, yet Quadratus never watched them, whether in the theatre or at home, and she did not require him to. Pliny recalls her telling him, when he was appointed to supervise her grandson's studies, that as a woman with a woman's idleness she used to relax by playing draughts or watching her pantomimes, but that whenever she was about to do either she would tell her grandson to go away and study — which seemed to Pliny to come from respect for the boy as much as affection. He adds that at the last games the actors were released and the crowd applauded them; Quadratus, who might have been thought to be enjoying it, showed no interest at all.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary. A rich letter for Roman social history: the status of pantomime performers, the moral policing of elite women, and the way Pliny simultaneously praises and patronises Ummidia.

lines.latin: Ummidia Quadratilla paulo minus octogensimo aetatis anno decessit usque ad novissimam valetudinem viridis, atque etiam ultra matronalem modum compacto corpore et robusto.
lines.english: Ummidia Quadratilla died a little short of her eightieth year of age, vigorous right up to her last illness, and even with a body compact and sturdy beyond the measure of a matron.

lines.latin: Decessit honestissimo testamento: reliquit heredes ex besse nepotem, ex tertia parte neptem. Neptem parum novi, nepotem familiarissime diligo, adulescentem singularem nec iis tantum, quos sanguine attingit, inter propinquos amandum.
lines.english: She died with a most honorable will: she left as heirs her grandson for two-thirds, her granddaughter for one third part. The granddaughter I know little; the grandson I love most intimately, a remarkable young man, and one to be loved among his relatives not only by those whom he touches by blood.

lines.latin: Ac primum conspicuus forma omnes sermones malignorum et puer et iuvenis evasit, intra quartum et vicensimum annum maritus, et si deus adnuisset pater. Vixit in contubernio aviae delicatae severissime, et tamen obsequentissime.
lines.english: And first, though conspicuous for his good looks, he escaped all the gossip of the malicious both as a boy and as a young man; within his twenty-fourth year [he was] a husband, and, if god had nodded assent, a father. He lived in the household of a pleasure-loving grandmother most strictly, and nevertheless most respectfully.

lines.latin: Habebat illa pantomimos fovebatque, effusius quam principi feminae convenit. Hos Quadratus non in theatro, non domi spectabat, nec illa exigebat.
lines.english: She kept pantomime actors and indulged them, more lavishly than suits a leading woman. These Quadratus did not watch in the theater, nor at home, nor did she demand it.

lines.latin: Audivi ipsam cum mihi commendaret nepotis sui studia, solere se, ut feminam in illo otio sexus, laxare animum lusu calculorum, solere spectare pantomimos suos, sed cum factura esset alterutrum, semper se nepoti suo praecepisse abiret studeretque; quod mihi non amore eius magis facere quam reverentia videbatur.
lines.english: I heard her herself, when she was entrusting to me her grandson’s studies, [say] that she, as a woman in the leisure of her sex, was accustomed to relax her mind with a game of counters, was accustomed to watch her pantomimes, but that, when she was about to do either, she always instructed her grandson to go away and study; which she seemed to me to do not more out of love for him than out of respect.

lines.latin: Miraberis, et ego miratus sum. Proximis sacerdotalibus ludis, productis in commissione pantomimis, cum simul theatro ego et Quadratus egrederemur, ait mihi: 'Scis me hodie primum vidisse saltantem aviae meae libertum?' Hoc nepos.
lines.english: You will be amazed, and I was amazed. At the most recent priestly games, when the pantomimes had been brought out in the opening show, as Quadratus and I were leaving the theater together, he says to me: “Do you know that today for the first time I have seen my grandmother’s freedman dancing?” This [said] the grandson.

lines.latin: At hercule alienissimi homines in honorem Quadratillae — pudet me dixisse honorem — per adulationis officium in theatrum cursitabant exsultabant plaudebant mirabantur ac deinde singulos gestus dominae cum canticis reddebant; qui nunc exiguissima legata, theatralis operae corollarium, accipient ab herede, qui non spectabat.
lines.english: But, by Hercules, the most unrelated men, in honor of Quadratilla — I am ashamed to have said “honor” — by the duty of flattery, were running about into the theater, were leaping up, were clapping, were marveling, and then were reproducing for their mistress each gesture with songs; who now will receive very small legacies, the tip for theatrical work, from an heir who used not to watch.

lines.latin: Haec, quia soles si quid incidit novi non invitus audire, deinde quia iucundum est mihi quod ceperam gaudium scribendo retractare. Gaudeo enim pietate defunctae, honore optimi iuvenis; laetor etiam quod domus aliquando C. Cassi, huius qui Cassianae scholae princeps et parens fuit, serviet domino non minori.
lines.english: These things [I write], because you are accustomed to hear, not unwillingly, if anything new has happened, then because it is pleasant for me to go over again by writing the joy which I had taken. For I rejoice at the dutifulness of the dead woman, at the honor of an excellent young man; I am glad also that the house once of Gaius Cassius, this [Cassius] who was the leader and father of the Cassian school, will serve a master no less.

lines.latin: Implebit enim illam Quadratus meus et decebit, rursusque ei pristinam dignitatem celebritatem gloriam reddet, cum tantus orator inde procedet, quantus iuris ille consultus. Vale.
lines.english: For my Quadratus will fill it and will be fitting for it, and again will give back to it its former dignity, fame, glory, when as great an orator will proceed from there as that man [was] an expert in law. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: The Chariot Races
summary: Pliny writes that he has spent all these recent days among his writing tablets and books in the most agreeable quiet. He asks how that was possible in the city — the Circus games were on, a kind of spectacle by which he is not in the least attracted: there is nothing new in it, nothing different, nothing that it is not enough to have seen once. He is therefore the more amazed that so many thousands of grown men should so childishly want again and again to see running horses and men standing in chariots. If they were drawn by the speed of the horses or the skill of the men there would be some reason in it; but in fact it is a strip of cloth they support, a strip of cloth they love, and if in the middle of the race the colours were swapped over, their enthusiasm and support would cross over with them, and they would suddenly abandon the drivers and the horses they recognise from far off and whose names they shout. Such is the influence and authority of one worthless tunic — not with the common crowd, which is worth less than a tunic, but with certain serious men. When he thinks that these people sit unwearied at so empty, so cold, so repetitive a business, he takes some pleasure in not being captured by that pleasure, and gladly gives to literature the days that others waste in the idlest occupations.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary. The classic elite Roman dismissal of the circus factions, and a good foil to the required letters on Roman social life. The rhetorical build (nihil novum, nihil varium, nihil...) is a clean example of anaphora and tricolon.

lines.latin: Omne hoc tempus inter pugillares ac libellos iucundissima quiete transmisi. 'Quemadmodum' inquis 'in urbe potuisti?' Circenses erant, quo genere spectaculi ne levissime quidem teneor. Nihil novum nihil varium, nihil quod non semel spectasse sufficiat.
lines.english: All this time I have spent among writing tablets and little books in the most pleasant quiet. “How,” you say, “were you able [to] in the city?” There were the circus games, by which kind of spectacle I am not held even very slightly. [There is] nothing new, nothing varied, nothing which it would not be enough to have watched once.

lines.latin: Quo magis miror tot milia virorum tam pueriliter identidem cupere currentes equos, insistentes curribus homines videre. Si tamen aut velocitate equorum aut hominum arte traherentur, esset ratio non nulla; nunc favent panno, pannum amant, et si in ipso cursu medioque certamine hic color illuc ille huc transferatur, studium favorque transibit, et repente agitatores illos equos illos, quos procul noscitant, quorum clamitant nomina relinquent.
lines.english: By which [fact] I wonder all the more that so many thousands of men so childishly desire again and again to see running horses, men standing on chariots. If, however, they were drawn either by the speed of the horses or by the skill of the men, there would be some reason; now they favor a cloth, they love a cloth, and if in the very race and in the middle of the contest this color were transferred there [and] that one here, their enthusiasm and favor will cross over, and suddenly they will abandon those drivers, those horses, which they recognize from afar, whose names they shout.

lines.latin: Tanta gratia tanta auctoritas in una vilissima tunica, mitto apud vulgus, quod vilius tunica, sed apud quosdam graves homines; quos ego cum recordor, in re inani frigida assidua, tam insatiabiliter desidere, capio aliquam voluptatem, quod hac voluptate non capior.
lines.english: So much favor, so much authority in one very cheap tunic — I pass over among the common crowd, which is cheaper than a tunic — but among certain serious men; and when I recall these men sitting so insatiably at a thing empty, cold, continual, I take some pleasure, because I am not taken by this pleasure.

lines.latin: Ac per hos dies libentissime otium meum in litteris colloco, quos alii otiosissimis occupationibus perdunt. Vale.
lines.english: And throughout these days I most gladly invest my leisure in literature, [days] which others waste in the idlest occupations. Farewell.

author: pliny
title: Trajan's Reply on the Aqueduct
summary: Trajan replies that care must be taken to bring water to Nicomedia, and he trusts Pliny will take up the matter with proper diligence. But it is equally part of that same diligence to find out through whose fault the people of Nicomedia have wasted so much money up to now — in case they have granted and abandoned aqueducts as a favour to one another. Whatever Pliny discovers, he is to bring it to Trajan's notice.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary. Trajan's insistence on identifying who wasted the money is characteristic of the tone of his replies, and a good short piece for translation practice.

lines.latin: Curandum est, ut aqua in Nicomedensem civitatem perducatur. Vere credo te ea, qua debebis, diligentia hoc opus aggressurum. Sed medius fidius ad eandem diligentiam tuam pertinet inquirere, quorum vitio ad hoc tempus tantam pecuniam Nicomedenses perdiderint, ne, dum inter se gratificantur, et incohaverint aquae ductus et reliquerint. Quid itaque compereris, perfer in notitiam meam.
lines.english: Care must be taken that water be brought into the city of Nicomedia. I truly believe that you will undertake this work with the diligence with which you ought. But, so help me heaven, it belongs to that same diligence of yours to inquire by whose fault the Nicomedians have wasted so much money up to this time, so that they do not, while doing favors for one another, both begin aqueducts and abandon them. Whatever, therefore, you find out, bring to my attention.

author: pliny
title: To Trajan: The Fire at Nicomedia
summary: Pliny reports that while he was travelling in another part of the province a very extensive fire at Nicomedia destroyed many private houses and two public buildings, the Gerusia and the temple of Isis, although a road lay between them. It spread more widely, first because of the violence of the wind and then because of the inertia of the people, who plainly stood by as idle and motionless spectators of so great a disaster. In any case there was not a single fire engine, not a bucket, nor any equipment for fighting fires anywhere in the community; these will now be provided on his orders. Pliny asks Trajan to consider whether a guild of firefighters should be established, limited to 150 men, since he will take care that only those of that trade are admitted and that the privilege granted is not used for any other purpose — and it will not be difficult to watch so few.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary, but it pairs directly with the required aqueduct letters as evidence of Pliny's provincial administration. Trajan's refusal in the reply (10.34) on the grounds that such associations become political clubs is one of the most historically important passages in Book 10.

lines.latin: Cum diversam partem provinciae circumirem, Nicomediae vastissimum incendium multas privatorum domos et duo publica opera, quamquam via interiacente, Gerusian et Iseon absumpsit.
lines.english: While I was going around a distant part of the province, a very vast fire at Nicomedia consumed many houses of private citizens and two public works, although a road lay between, the Gerusia and the Iseum.

lines.latin: Est autem latius sparsum, primum violentia venti, deinde inertia hominum quos satis constat otiosos et immobiles tanti mali spectatores perstitisse; et alioqui nullus usquam in publico sipo, nulla hama, nullum denique instrumentum ad incendia compescenda. Et haec quidem, ut iam praecepi, parabuntur;
lines.english: It spread more widely, however, first by the violence of the wind, then by the inactivity of the people, who, it is well agreed, stood by idle and motionless, spectators of so great a disaster; and besides [there was] nowhere in public any pump, no bucket, finally no equipment for putting out fires. And these things indeed, as I have already instructed, will be provided;

lines.latin: tu, domine, dispice an instituendum putes collegium fabrorum dumtaxat hominum CL. Ego attendam, ne quis nisi faber recipiatur neve iure concesso in aliud utantur; nec erit difficile custodire tam paucos.
lines.english: you, lord, consider whether you think that a guild of firemen should be established, of only 150 men. I will see to it that no one except a fireman is admitted, and that they do not use the right granted for another [purpose]; nor will it be difficult to watch over so few.

author: pliny
title: Trajan's Reply: No Firefighters' Guild
summary: Trajan replies that it has occurred to Pliny, following the example of many others, that a guild of firefighters could be set up at Nicomedia. But it must be remembered that that province, and especially those cities, have been troubled by factions of this kind. Whatever name and for whatever reason he gives to those gathered together, they will nonetheless become political clubs within a short time. It is therefore better to provide the equipment that can help against fires, and to warn property owners to check the fires themselves, and, if the situation requires it, to make use of the assembled populace.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary. Historically one of the most cited passages in Book 10: an emperor refusing a fire brigade because any association is a potential political threat. It is the clearest statement of imperial suspicion of collegia.

lines.latin: Tibi quidem secundum exempla complurium in mentem venit posse collegium fabrorum apud Nicomedenses constitui. Sed meminerimus provinciam istam et praecipue eas civitates eius modi factionibus esse vexatas. Quodcumque nomen ex quacumque causa dederimus iis, qui in idem contracti fuerint, hetaeriae eaeque brevi fient.
lines.english: It has occurred to you, indeed, following the examples of very many [places], that a guild of firemen could be established among the Nicomedians. But let us remember that that province, and especially those cities, have been troubled by factions of this kind. Whatever name, for whatever reason, we give to those who have been brought together for the same [purpose], they will become political clubs, and quickly.

lines.latin: Satius itaque est comparari ea, quae ad coercendos ignes auxilio esse possint, admonerique dominos praediorum, ut et ipsi inhibeant ac, si res poposcerit, accursu populi ad hoc uti.
lines.english: It is better, therefore, that those things be provided which can be of help for controlling fires, and that the owners of properties be advised both to check [them] themselves and, if the situation demands, to use the crowd running together for this.

author: pliny
title: To Trajan: Unfinished Buildings at Nicaea and Claudiopolis
summary: Pliny reports that the theatre at Nicaea, largely built but unfinished, has already consumed more than ten million sesterces — he fears in vain, since it is settling and showing huge cracks, either because the ground is damp and soft or because the stone itself is poor and crumbling. It is worth considering whether it should be finished, abandoned, or even demolished, since the substructures and foundations meant to hold it up seem more costly than solid. Many parts were promised by private individuals — basilicas around it, a colonnade above the seating — all now deferred since the main work stands still. The same people have also begun to rebuild, before Pliny's arrival, a gymnasium destroyed by fire, on a larger and more scattered plan; they have already spent a good deal, and Pliny fears to less purpose, since the buildings are incoherent and disorganised. An architect, admittedly a rival of the one who began it, maintains that the walls, though twenty-two feet thick, cannot support the weight placed on them, because they are packed with rubble and not faced with brickwork. The people of Claudiopolis are meanwhile digging out rather than building an enormous bath at the foot of a mountain, using money that the councillors whom Trajan added to the senate have paid or will pay at Pliny's direction. Fearing that public money at Nicaea and, what is dearer than any money, Trajan's own gift at Claudiopolis may be badly spent, he asks the emperor to send an architect to inspect both the theatre and the bath and decide what is best.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary. It is the fullest surviving account of provincial building projects going wrong, and the professional rivalry between architects is a rare detail. It pairs closely with the required aqueduct letter 10.37.

lines.latin: Theatrum, domine, Nicaeae maxima iam parte constructum, imperfectum tamen, sestertium - ut audio; neque enim ratio operis excussa est - amplius centies hausit: vereor ne frustra.
lines.english: The theater at Nicaea, lord, already built for the greatest part, yet unfinished, has swallowed up more than ten million sesterces — as I hear; for the account of the work has not been examined —: I fear [it has been] in vain.

lines.latin: Ingentibus enim rimis desedit et hiat, sive in causa solum umidum et molle, sive lapis ipse gracilis et putris: dignum est certe deliberatione, sitne faciendum an sit relinquendum an etiam destruendum. Nam fulturae ac substructiones, quibus subinde suscipitur, non tam firmae mihi quam sumptuosae uidentur.
lines.english: For it has settled and gapes with huge cracks, whether the cause [is] the soil, damp and soft, or the stone itself, thin and crumbling: it is certainly worthy of deliberation whether it should be finished or should be abandoned or even demolished. For the supports and substructures by which it is propped up from time to time seem to me not so much firm as costly.

lines.latin: Huic theatro ex priuatorum pollicitationibus multa debentur, ut basilicae circa, ut porticus supra caveam. Quae nunc omnia differuntur cessante eo, quod ante peragendum est.
lines.english: To this theater many things are owed from the promises of private citizens, such as basilicas around [it], such as a colonnade above the seating. All of which are now put off, since that [work] is at a standstill which must be completed first.

lines.latin: Iidem Nicaeenses gymnasium incendio amissum ante aduentum meum restituere coeperunt, longe numerosius laxiusque quam fuerat, et iam aliquantum erogauerunt; periculum est, ne parum utiliter; incompositum enim et sparsum est. Praeterea architectus, sane aemulus eius a quo opus incohatum est, adfirmat parietes quamquam uiginti et duos pedes latos imposita onera sustinere non posse, quia sine caemento medii farti nec testaceo opere praecincti.
lines.english: The same Nicaeans began to restore the gymnasium, lost in a fire before my arrival, far more extensive and spacious than it had been, and they have already paid out a considerable amount; there is a danger [that it has been] to little use; for it is ill-planned and scattered. Moreover the architect, certainly a rival of the one by whom the work was begun, asserts that the walls, although twenty-two feet wide, cannot support the loads placed upon them, because they are stuffed in the middle without cement and not faced with brickwork.

lines.latin: Claudiopolitani quoque in depresso loco, imminente etiam monte ingens balineum defodiunt magis quam aedificant, et quidem ex ea pecunia, quam buleutae additi beneficio tuo aut iam obtulerunt ob introitum aut nobis exigentibus conferent.
lines.english: The people of Claudiopolis also, in a low-lying place, with a mountain even overhanging, are digging out rather than building a huge bath, and indeed from that money which the councillors added by your favor either have already offered for their admission or will contribute at our demanding.

lines.latin: Ergo cum timeam ne illic publica pecunia, hic, quod est omni pecunia pretiosius, munus tuum male collocetur, cogor petere a te non solum ob theatrum, uerum etiam ob haec balinea mittas architectum, dispecturum utrum sit utilius post sumptum qui factus est quoquo modo consummare opera? ut incohata sunt, an quae uidentur emendanda corrigere, quae transferenda transferre, ne dum servare uolumus quod impensum est, male impendamus quod addendum est.
lines.english: Therefore, since I fear that in the one place public money, in the other, what is more precious than all money, your gift, may be badly invested, I am compelled to ask you to send an architect not only for the theater but also for these baths, to examine whether it is more useful, after the expense which has been made, to complete the works in whatever way, as they have been begun, or to correct those things which seem to need amending, to move those which [seem] to need moving, so that, while we wish to save what has been spent, we do not spend badly what must be added.

author: pliny
title: Trajan's Reply on the Buildings
summary: Trajan replies that what should be done about the theatre begun at Nicaea can best be decided by Pliny on the spot. It will be enough for Trajan to be told what he decides. He adds that Pliny should require the private contributions from individuals once the theatre, for whose sake they were promised, is complete. He remarks that those little Greeks are fond of gymnasia — so perhaps the people of Nicaea have laid out their plans too ambitiously; but they must be content with what is enough for their needs. On the bath at Claudiopolis, which he says they have begun in a poorly chosen spot, Pliny must decide what advice to give. Architects cannot be lacking to him: no province is without both skilled and clever men — unless one supposes it quicker to send them from Rome, when in fact they usually come to us from Greece.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — supplementary. Notable for Trajan's dismissive Graeculi ('those little Greeks') and for the closing observation that architects come to Rome from Greece — useful evidence for Roman attitudes to Greek culture and provincial expertise.

lines.latin: Quid oporteat fieri circa theatrum, quod incohatum apud Nicaeenses est, in re praesenti optime deliberabis et constitues. Mihi sufficiet indicari, cui sententiae accesseris: Tunc autem a priuatis exige opera, cum theatrum, propter quod illa promissa sunt, factum erit.
lines.english: What ought to be done about the theater which has been begun among the Nicaeans, you will best deliberate and decide on the spot. It will be enough for me to be told which opinion you have adopted. Then, however, demand the works from the private citizens, when the theater, on account of which those things were promised, has been finished.

lines.latin: Gymnasiis indulgent Graeculi; ideo forsitan Nicaeenses maiore animo constructionem eius aggressi sunt: sed oportet illos eo contentos esse, quod possit illis sufficere.
lines.english: The little Greeks indulge in gymnasia; for that reason perhaps the Nicaeans undertook its construction with too great ambition: but they ought to be content with that which can be enough for them.

lines.latin: Quid Claudiopolitanis circa balineum quod parum, ut scribis, idoneo loco incohauerunt suadendum sit, tu constitues. Architecti tibi deesse non possunt. Nulla prouincia non et peritos et ingeniosos homines habet; modo ne existimes breuius esse ab urbe mitti, cum ex Graecia etiam ad nos uenire soliti sint.
lines.english: What should be recommended to the people of Claudiopolis about the bath, which they have begun in a place, as you write, hardly suitable, you will decide. You cannot lack architects. There is no province which does not have both skilled and talented men; only do not think that it is quicker for one to be sent from the City, since they are accustomed to come even to us from Greece.

author: vergil
title: Juno and Aeolus
summary: Barely out of sight of Sicily and sailing for the open sea, the Trojans draw Juno's undying anger. Brooding on her thwarted love for Carthage and the old grievances — the Judgement of Paris, Ganymede, her failed war at Troy — she cannot understand why she still fails to keep one race from Italy. She seeks out Aeolus, king of the winds, in his mountain prison of storms, and bribes him with marriage to her loveliest nymph, Deiopea, in exchange for sinking the Trojan fleet. Aeolus, who owes his very throne and scepter to Jupiter's favor toward Juno, agrees at once and drives his spear into the mountainside, loosing the winds upon the sea.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list. Included here as the connective narrative between the two readings that are (1.1–33 and 1.88–107) — Juno's monologue of grievance and her bargain with Aeolus are what actually sets the storm of 1.88ff. in motion, so the opening of the poem reads as one continuous scene rather than jumping straight from the proem to the storm's first line. Aeolus's cave (52–63), ruling wind and sea by another's leave, is itself a miniature of the poem's central tension between furor and imperium.

author: vergil
title: The Ghost of Hector
summary: It was the hour when first rest begins for weary mortals and creeps over them as the gods' most welcome gift. In sleep Hector appeared before Aeneas' eyes, deeply mourning and pouring floods of tears — as he had been when dragged by the chariot, black with bloody dust, his swollen feet pierced by thongs. He was not the Hector who returned wearing Achilles' spoils or after hurling Trojan fire on the Greek ships, but filthy in beard, his hair matted with blood, bearing the many wounds he received around his native walls. Aeneas weeps and questions him; Hector gives no answer to his idle questions but tells him to flee, that the enemy holds the walls, that Troy is falling from her high summit. Enough has been given to Priam and country: if Pergama could have been defended by any hand, it would have been defended by his. Troy entrusts to Aeneas her sacred things and her household gods; he is to take them as companions of his fate and seek for them the great city that he will at last establish after wandering the sea.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — this passage was required under the previous (2012–2025) AP Latin syllabus. Included here as supplementary reading. It is nonetheless one of the best examples in the poem of a dream vision and of the transfer of the Penates that founds Rome's religious continuity.

author: vergil
title: Mercury's Message
summary: Mercury finds Aeneas founding towers and building houses, wearing a sword starred with tawny jasper and a cloak of Tyrian purple that Dido had made. He rebukes him at once: is he now laying foundations for lofty Carthage, a husband building a fine city, forgetful of his own kingdom and affairs? The ruler of the gods sends this message himself — what does Aeneas plan, on what hope does he waste time in Libyan lands? If no glory in such great affairs moves him, let him look to growing Ascanius and to the hopes of his heir Iulus, to whom the kingdom of Italy and the Roman land are owed. Mercury vanishes into thin air. Aeneas is struck dumb and out of his mind, his hair standing on end and his voice sticking in his throat; he burns to flee and leave the sweet lands, thunderstruck by so great a warning. He turns over what to do, how to approach the queen, and settles on summoning his captains to prepare the fleet in secret while he seeks the best moment to speak.

author: vergil
title: Charon and the Unburied Dead
summary: From here is the road to the waters of Tartarean Acheron; a whirlpool boils with mud and vast depths and belches all its sand into Cocytus. A dreadful ferryman guards these waters and streams, Charon, terrible in his squalor, with a mass of unkempt grey beard, staring eyes, a filthy cloak knotted from his shoulders. He poles the boat himself, tends the sails and carries the dead in his rust-coloured skiff — old now, but a god's old age is green and raw. Here the whole crowd rushed streaming to the banks, mothers and men and the bodies of great-hearted heroes finished with life, boys and unmarried girls, and young men placed on pyres before their parents' eyes — as many as the leaves that fall in the woods at the first frost of autumn, or as many as the birds that flock to land from the deep when the cold season drives them across the sea to sunny countries. They stood begging to cross first, stretching out their hands in longing for the far bank; but the grim sailor takes now these, now those, and pushes others back far from the sand. The Sibyl explains that those buried may cross, while the helpless and unburied must wander a hundred years before they may return and revisit the longed-for pools.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — required under the previous AP Latin syllabus. The paired leaf and bird similes (6.309–312) are among the most famous in Latin poetry and are frequently used for style questions.

author: vergil
title: Crossing the Styx and Cerberus
summary: As they continue their journey and approach the river, the ferryman sees them from the Stygian wave coming through the silent wood and turning their steps to the bank, and challenges them: whoever they are, they should stop where they are and say why they come armed. This is the place of shades, of Sleep and drowsy Night; it is not lawful to carry living bodies in the Stygian boat, and he had no joy of receiving Hercules, Theseus and Pirithous, sons of gods though they were. The Sibyl answers briefly that there is no such trickery here, that the weapons bring no violence, and that Aeneas, famous for piety, goes down to his father in the deepest shadows of Erebus; if so great an image of piety moves him nothing, let him at least recognise the bough — and she shows the branch hidden in her robe. Charon's swelling anger settles; he admires the fateful rod, turns the stern about and brings the boat to shore, ships out the other souls, takes on the great Aeneas, and the seamed boat groans under the weight and takes in marsh water through its chinks. At last he lands them safely on the far bank in formless mud and grey sedge. Huge Cerberus, with his three throats, lies in a cave opposite, barking; the Sibyl throws him a sop drugged with honey and medicated grain, and the beast opens his three mouths, swallows it, relaxes his monstrous back and sprawls over the whole cave, so that Aeneas seizes the entrance and passes.

author: vergil
title: Marcellus and the Gates of Sleep
summary: Anchises continues, pointing out Marcellus advancing distinguished by the spoils of a chief and towering as victor over all. He will steady the Roman state when it is shaken by a great uprising, will lay low the Carthaginian and the rebellious Gaul, and will dedicate the third set of captured arms to father Quirinus. Aeneas, seeing beside him a youth outstanding in appearance and shining arms, but with a face of little cheer and downcast eyes, asks who accompanies him — a son, or one of the great line of his descendants? What a noise of companions about him, and what a presence he has, but black night flies about his head with its mournful shade. Anchises, with welling tears, tells him not to ask about the great grief of his people: the fates will only show him to the earth and not allow him to remain longer. He laments the boy — if he could break the harsh fates, he would be Marcellus — and asks for lilies in armfuls, to scatter purple flowers and heap at least these gifts on his descendant's shade. So they wander through the whole region in the wide airy fields and survey everything. When Anchises has led his son through each place and fired his soul with love of the fame to come, he tells him of the wars that must be waged, of the Laurentine peoples and the city of Latinus, and how he is to flee or bear each labour. There are two gates of Sleep, one said to be of horn, by which true shades are given easy exit, the other gleaming with polished white ivory — but through it the spirits send false dreams to the world above. With these words Anchises accompanies his son and the Sibyl and sends them out by the ivory gate. Aeneas makes his way to the ships and rejoins his companions, then holds his course straight along the shore to the harbour of Caieta.

author: catullus
title: Let Us Live and Love
summary: Catullus urges Lesbia to live and love with him, and to value the disapproving gossip of stern old men at only a single penny. The sun can set and rise again, but once their own brief light sets, humans face one unending night of sleep. He asks her for a thousand kisses, then a hundred, then another thousand, then a second hundred — on and on in a deliberately uncountable heap — so that once they have made many thousands together, they can mix the count up and lose track, so that neither they themselves nor any envious enemy who learns the true number can put the evil eye on so many kisses.
context: NOT on the official 2025 CED required reading list — the syllabus is fixed to Vergil and Pliny — but placed here in Unit 6 ("Course Project and Teacher's Choice Poetry") as one of the most famous and most frequently taught short poems in the entire Latin corpus. Written in hendecasyllabic metre (eleven syllables per line), not the Aeneid's dactylic hexameter, so it is not included in the Scansion Lab, which is built specifically around hexameter. The poem's closing image — deliberately losing count of the kisses — plays on a real Roman superstition: naming an exact large number let an envious enemy cast the evil eye (invidere) on exactly what you had, so the lovers scramble the sum on purpose.

author: other
title: Why the Boy Hated Greek
summary: Augustine asks why, as a boy, he hated Greek grammar, which "sang" the same kind of stories he loved in Latin. Homer is skilled at weaving tales and is delightfully hollow, yet to the young Augustine he was bitter, and he supposes Vergil is just as bitter to Greek boys forced to learn him the way he was forced to learn Homer. The difficulty of learning a foreign language at all sprinkled gall, as it were, over all the Greek sweetness of the stories: he knew none of the words, and he was pressed hard, with savage threats and punishments, to learn them. Latin, by contrast, he had picked up as an infant without fear or torment, just by paying attention, among the coaxing of nurses, the jokes of people smiling at him and the fun of people playing with him. His conclusion: free curiosity has more power to make us learn than fearful compulsion.
context: One of College Board's four Course Project passages for 2025–26 (prose), kept here for practice. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 CE) was born in Roman North Africa and became a bishop and one of the most influential Christian thinkers in the West. The Confessions, written in the late 390s, tell the story of his life up to his conversion as a long address to God, which is why the narrator keeps stepping back from an anecdote to ask what it means. Here the anecdote is his own schooling: Roman boys learned Greek from a grammaticus, by memorisation and the rod. Watch how the argument is built: a question (Cur...?), a paradox (dulcissime vanus... amarus), an analogy with Vergil, a contrast between the two languages (Greek with poenis, Latin sine poenis) and a closing maxim. Lines 1–9 and 10–15 are almost mirror images of each other, and the vocabulary of pleasure (dulcissime, suavitates, blandimenta, ioca, laetitias) is set against the vocabulary of pain (amarus, felle, terroribus, poenis, cruciatu).

author: other
title: A Wife Who Saved Her Husband
summary: A husband speaks to his dead wife. When he had to flee, she gave him the fullest help: she equipped him for the journey by taking off all her gold and pearls and handing them to him, and then, slipping past the guards his enemies had set, kept sending him slaves, money and supplies, so that his absence was well provided for. She pleaded for his life while he was away, as her courage urged her to, and her words won him the mercy of the very men she was working against; her voice never lost its firmness. Meanwhile, when a band of men gathered by Milo (whose house the husband had bought while Milo was in exile) tried to use the chances of civil war to break in and loot it, she drove them back and defended their home.
context: One of College Board's four Course Project passages for 2025–26 (prose), kept here for practice. The "Laudatio Turiae" is a long funerary inscription from the late first century BCE, a husband's address to his late wife. Her real name is lost (Turia is a modern identification), and so is his. This section is set in 49 BCE, at the start of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey, when the husband, on Pompey's side, had to go into hiding. It is an inscription, not literature written for readers, so the Latin is plain and sometimes clipped, but it is shaped with care: almost every sentence has the wife as its subject and a second-person perfect verb (praestitisti, instruxisti, tradidisti, locupletasti, reiecisti, defendisti), so the husband's praise reads as a list of her deeds. The imperfects (rogabas, hortabatur, munibat, parabas) mark what she kept doing over time. Titus Annius Milo had been exiled in 52 BCE for the killing of Clodius; the "posse" in lines 9–11 is a gang trying to take back his former house.

author: other
title: Arion and the Dolphin
summary: Every sea and land knows Arion, whose song could hold back running water; wolf and lamb alike stopped to listen. Sailing home with the wealth his art had won, he might have feared the winds and waves, but the sea was safer than his own ship: the helmsman stood over him with a drawn sword, and the rest of the crew, in on the plot, were armed too. Terrified, Arion says he does not beg for his life, only to be allowed to take up his lyre and play a little first. They grant it and laugh at the delay. He puts on a crown fit for Apollo's hair and a robe twice dyed in Tyrian purple, and sings a mournful song, like a swan pierced by an arrow singing for the last time. Then he leaps, fully dressed, into the sea. A dolphin, the story goes (hard to believe), put its curved back under its strange load, and Arion rode it, holding his lyre and singing as his fare, calming the waters with his song.
context: One of College Board's four Course Project passages for 2025–26 (poetry), kept here for practice. Ovid (43 BCE–17 CE) wrote the Fasti as a poem on the Roman calendar, explaining festivals and the stars that rise on each day. Arion's story comes under February 3, when the constellation Delphinus, the Dolphin, sets. The tale is old (Herodotus tells it): a famous singer from Lesbos, on his way back to Corinth from a tour of Italy and Sicily, robbed by the sailors and saved by a dolphin. The metre is elegiac couplets, a dactylic hexameter followed by a pentameter, which you scan exactly as you scan Vergil for the hexameter lines. Ovid addresses Arion directly (infelix, line 7) and Apollo (Phoebe, line 14), and he keeps reminding you that song controls nature: carmine in lines 2 and 24 frames the passage. Note the swan simile (lines 17–18), the irony that the sea was safer than the ship (line 8), and the narrator's wink that the rescue is fide maius (line 21).

author: other
title: A Game of Chess with the King
summary: Ruodlieb tells the story himself. The king calls for the board, has a seat set opposite him and orders Ruodlieb to sit facing him on a couch and play. Ruodlieb tries hard to refuse: it is a frightful thing, he says, for a poor man to play against a king. When the king sees that he does not dare refuse him, Ruodlieb gives in and praises the game, hoping to be beaten: what harm is there in a poor man losing to a king? His fear is the opposite: if luck helps him and the victory goes his way, the king will soon be angry with him. The king smiles and jokes: there is nothing to fear; even if he never wins he will not get angry. He wants Ruodlieb to play as seriously as he knows how, because he wants to learn the moves he does not know. They both play eagerly, and (thanks be to Victory) Ruodlieb wins three times, while the king's nobles look on in great amazement.
context: One of College Board's four Course Project passages for 2025–26 (poetry), kept here for practice. The Ruodlieb is an eleventh-century Latin poem from Germany, probably by a monk, about a young knight who leaves home to serve a foreign king; it is one of the first romances in European literature and is unusually realistic about courtly life. This scene is among the earliest descriptions of chess in Europe. The metre is the Leonine hexameter: an ordinary dactylic hexameter whose middle and end rhyme, sometimes loosely (tabulam / sellam in line 1, ludam / renuebam in line 3, laudavi / superari in line 6). Medieval Latin shows here and there: de rege for the agent (line 7), quod clauses after timeo (lines 8–9), gerunds used as present participles (subridendo, iocando, line 10), haut for haud and commocior for commotior (line 12). The humour is in the reversal: the guest who wants to lose, the king who wants to learn, and the guest's victory credited, politely, to Lady Victory rather than to himself.
